title: HNF-6 Genetic Variability and Its Association with Type II Diabetes and Insulin Secretion
abstract: Hepatocyte nuclear factor-6 : associations between genetic variability and type II diabetes and between genetic variability and estimates of insulin secretion. The transcription factor hepatocyte nuclear factor (HNF)-6 is an upstream regulator of several genes involved in the pathogenesis of maturity-onset diabetes of the young. We therefore tested the hypothesis that variability in the HNF-6 gene is associated with subsets of Type II (non-insulin-dependent) diabetes mellitus and estimates of insulin secretion in glucose tolerant subjects. We cloned the coding region as well as the intron-exon boundaries of the HNF-6 gene. We then examined them on genomic DNA in six MODY probands without mutations in the MODY1, MODY3 and MODY4 genes and in 54 patients with late-onset Type II diabetes by combined single strand conformational polymorphism-heteroduplex analysis followed by direct sequencing of identified variants. An identified missense variant was examined in association studies and genotype-phenotype studies. We identified two silent and one missense (Pro75 Ala) variant. In an association study the allelic frequency of the Pro75Ala polymorphism was 3.2% (95% confidence interval, 1.9 - 4.5) in 330 patients with Type II diabetes mellitus compared with 4.2% (2.4 - 6.0) in 238 age-matched glucose tolerant control subjects. Moreover, in studies of 238 middle-aged glucose tolerant subjects, of 226 glucose tolerant offspring of Type II diabetic patients and of 367 young healthy subjects, the carriers of the polymorphism did not differ from non-carriers in glucose induced serum insulin or C-peptide responses. Mutations in the coding region of the HNF-6 gene are not associated with Type II diabetes or with changes in insulin responses to glucose among the Caucasians examined.

title: Mannose-Binding Protein and Langerin in Langerhans Cell Function
abstract: Langerin, a novel C-type lectin specific to Langerhans cells, is an endocytic receptor that induces the formation of Birbeck granules. We have identified a type II Ca2+-dependent lectin displaying mannose-binding specificity, exclusively expressed by Langerhans cells (LC), and named Langerin. LC are uniquely characterized by Birbeck granules (BG), which are organelles consisting of superimposed and zippered membranes. Here, we have shown that Langerin is constitutively associated with BG and that antibody to Langerin is internalized into these structures. Remarkably, transfection of Langerin cDNA into fibroblasts created a compact network of membrane structures with typical features of BG. Langerin is thus a potent inducer of membrane superimposition and zippering leading to BG formation. Our data suggest that induction of BG is a consequence of the antigen-capture function of Langerin, allowing routing into these organelles and providing access to a nonclassical antigen-processing pathway. Mannose-binding, a key feature of Langerin, facilitates the specific recognition and internalization of antigens by Langerhans cells.

title: Efficacy and Safety of Subcutaneous Apomorphine in Parkinson's Disease Management
abstract: Apomorphine has emerged as a valuable alternative for managing Parkinson's disease, particularly in patients experiencing fluctuating symptoms. As one of the earliest dopaminergic drugs employed in Parkinson's treatment, apomorphine has demonstrated significant antiparkinsonian effects since its initial use in 1951. Recent studies have highlighted the effectiveness of subcutaneous apomorphine injections in providing comparable benefits to levodopa, with rescue injections effectively addressing off-periods in patients with complex motor fluctuations. Continuous subcutaneous infusions of apomorphine have been shown to reduce daily off-time by over 50%, outperforming conventional add-on therapies with oral dopamine agonists or COMT inhibitors. Long-term follow-up data spanning up to 8 years confirm sustained efficacy. Notably, monotherapy with continuous infusions significantly reduces levodopa-induced dyskinesias. While cutaneous tolerability issues are the primary side effects, psychiatric complications and sedation are less commonly observed. This treatment approach, with its marked efficacy in fluctuating Parkinson's disease, warrants broader clinical implementation. Additional indexed biomedical mentions considered for relation extraction included: Parkinson 's disease; dopaminergic drug.

title: Rab6c, a Novel Rab Gene Family Member, Is Involved in Drug Resistance in Breast Cancer and Uterine Sarcoma Cells
abstract: Rab6c, a new member of the Rab gene family, was identified as a potential regulator of drug resistance in MCF7/AdrR cells. A Rab6 homolog cDNA, Rab6c, was discovered using a hypermethylated DNA fragment probe derived from a human multidrug-resistant (MDR) breast cancer cell line, MCF7/AdrR, through methylation-sensitive representational difference analysis (MS-RDA). Rab6c was found to be under-expressed in MCF7/AdrR and MES-SA/Dx5 (a human MDR uterine sarcoma cell line) compared to their non-MDR parental lines. Transfectants expressing exogenous Rab6c showed reduced resistance to several chemotherapeutic agents, including doxorubicin, taxol, vinblastine, and vincristine, compared to control cells. Flow cytometry confirmed that Rab6c overexpression enhanced drug accumulation in MCF7/AdrR cells, suggesting a role in drug sensitivity. These findings indicate that Rab6c is associated with drug resistance in both breast cancer and uterine sarcoma contexts, with a positive correlation between Rab6c expression and responsiveness to vincristine.

title: Calcineurin Inhibitors and Renal Complications in Liver Transplantation
abstract: Patients undergoing orthotopic liver transplantation (OLTX) often experience complications related to calcineurin-based immunosuppression. Cyclosporine and tacrolimus, two commonly used calcineurin inhibitors, are associated with nephrotoxic effects. This study investigates the prevalence and management of end-stage renal disease (ESRD) and chronic renal failure (CRF) in OLTX recipients. The research included 834 patients who survived at least six months post-transplantation, divided into three groups: controls without CRF/ESRD, CRF patients with elevated serum creatinine levels, and ESRD patients. Findings indicate that 18.1% of patients developed severe renal dysfunction, with CRF and ESRD rates at 8.6% and 9.5%, respectively. ESRD patients showed higher preoperative serum creatinine, greater hepatorenal syndrome prevalence, and increased dialysis needs. Serum creatinine levels post-transplantation were significant predictors of CRF/ESRD development. While overall survival was similar across groups, ESRD patients had a 28.2% survival rate at 13 years, compared to 54.6% in controls. Dialysis-only treatment significantly reduced ESRD survival, highlighting the need for improved long-term immunosuppressive strategies.

title: Late-Onset Metachromatic Leukodystrophy: Genetic and Molecular Insights
abstract: A novel mutation at the arylsulfatase A (ARSA) locus was identified in two siblings diagnosed with late-onset metachromatic leukodystrophy (MLD). This mutation involves the substitution of arginine84 with glutamine, a change that occurs in a highly conserved residue within the arylsulfatase gene family. Unlike earlier mutations associated with early-onset MLD, this alteration is linked to partial ARSA activity. Comparative analysis of genotypes, ARSA activity levels, and clinical data across 4 individuals with this mutation, alongside 81 patients with MLD, supports the hypothesis that varying degrees of residual ARSA activity contribute to the phenotypic diversity observed in MLD.

title: Mutations in the PCSK9 Gene and Their Association with Hypercholesterolemia in Norwegian Patients
abstract: Mutations in the PCSK9 gene were identified in Norwegian patients with autosomal dominant hypercholesterolemia. Proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9) is associated with autosomal dominant hypercholesterolemia, and recent studies suggest its involvement in cholesterol metabolism. Genetic analysis of the PCSK9 gene in 51 Norwegian individuals with familial hypercholesterolemia revealed mutations in the low-density lipoprotein receptor gene and R3500Q in the apolipoprotein B-100 gene were excluded. Two novel missense mutations were detected in the PCSK9 gene, including D374Y and N157 K. D374Y mutations were found to correlate with autosomal dominant hypercholesterolemia in two families, while one patient exhibited a double heterozygote for D374Y and N157 K. Cholesterol levels were observed to be elevated in patients harboring D374Y mutations, supporting the role of PCSK9 in lipid homeostasis. The apolipoprotein B-100 gene variant D374Y was linked to hypercholesterolemia, and the N157 K mutation was associated with altered LDL receptor function. These findings reinforce the connection between PCSK9 mutations and hypercholesterolemia, highlighting the genetic basis of this condition.

title: Molecular and Clinical Features of Desmin-Related Myopathies and Associated Genetic Mutations
abstract: A specific type of myopathy linked to Mallory-like inclusions is associated with mutations in the selenoprotein N gene. Desmin-related myopathies (DRMs) represent a diverse group of muscle disorders characterized by intracellular aggregates of desmin. Genetic mutations in the desmin and alpha-B crystallin genes are implicated in approximately one-third of DRM cases. The molecular basis of the remaining cases remains unclear, including an early-onset, recessive variant with Mallory body-like inclusions (MB-DRMs), first described in a German family. Recent studies identified the selenoprotein N gene (SEPN1) as the cause of SEPN-related myopathy (SEPN-RM), a condition previously classified into two distinct categories: rigid spine muscular dystrophy and severe multiminicore disease. The presence of Mallory-like inclusions in SEPN-RM cases suggested a potential link between MB-DRMs and SEPN1. In the original German family, a linkage to the SEPN1 locus (1p36) was confirmed, along with a homozygous SEPN1 deletion (del 92 nucleotide -19/+73) in affected individuals. Comparative analysis revealed identical clinical features between MB-DRMs and SEPN-RM, leading to the proposal that MB-DRMs should be reclassified as SEPN-RM. These findings highlight the genetic heterogeneity of DRMs, expand the phenotypic spectrum of SEPN-RM, and emphasize the need to reassess diagnostic criteria for early-onset myopathies. Additionally, muscle disorders are associated with multiple genetic factors, including the selenoprotein N gene and desmin, underscoring the complexity of these conditions. Additional indexed biomedical mentions considered for relation extraction included: Desmin-related myopathy.

title: Replication Timing Abnormalities in HIRA/Tuple1 and Phenotypic Features in DGS/VCFS
abstract: Abnormal replication timing of the HIRA/Tuple1 locus is observed in patients with cardiovascular , craniofacial , and thymic malformations , as well as in those with DiGeorge and Velocardiofacial syndromes . The latter condition is characterized by heterozygous deletions of the 22q11 chromosomal region . The Typically Deleted Region in the 22q11.21 subband (TDR22 ) contains multiple genes , including HIRA/Tuple1 , which maps to the non-deleted portion of this region . Studies have shown that the deletion extent is well-defined , yet the mechanism underlying the DGS/VCFS phenotype remains unclear . Our findings demonstrate that HIRA/Tuple1 in DGS/VCFS patients exhibits delayed replication timing , and that the locus is more frequently localized to the nuclear periphery . Replication timing and nuclear location are generally linked to transcriptional activity of the DNA region . These alterations in the TDR22 region suggest potential changes in gene regulation and transcription , which may contribute to the complex phenotypic features observed in DGS/VCFS and cardiovascular , craniofacial , and thymic malformations .

title: Catecholamine-Induced Cardiomyopathy and Myocardial Dysfunction
abstract: A 42-year-old man presented with acute myocardial stunning following an accidental epinephrine injection during a routine procedure. The patient developed severe left ventricular systolic and diastolic dysfunction, consistent with catecholamine-induced cardiomyopathy. Despite the transient nature of the condition, the episode highlighted the risks associated with excessive catecholamine exposure. Catecholamine-induced myocardial stunning was observed alongside cardiomyopathy, with no direct correlation between the two conditions. Epinephrine administration led to significant hemodynamic instability, emphasizing the need for careful dosing and monitoring in clinical settings.

title: Evaluating Cardiovascular Risks of COX-2 Inhibitors in Arthritis Patients
abstract: The effects of valdecoxib, a cyclooxygenase-2-specific inhibitor, were compared to nonsteroidal antiinflammatory agents and placebo in patients with arthritis. Concerns about increased cardiovascular thrombotic events with COX-2-specific inhibitors compared to nonselective NSAIDs were addressed by analyzing data from 10 randomized clinical trials involving approximately 8000 patients with osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis. The incidence of cardiovascular thrombotic events, including cardiac, cerebrovascular, and peripheral vascular events, was assessed in patients treated with valdecoxib (10-80 mg daily), nonselective NSAIDs (diclofenac 75 mg bid, ibuprofen 800 mg tid, naproxen 500 mg bid), and placebo. Incidence rates were similar across all treatment groups, with valdecoxib, NSAIDs, and placebo showing comparable risk profiles. Aspirin users had a higher thrombotic risk compared to nonusers, with rates of 1.4% for placebo, 1.7% for valdecoxib, and 1.9% for NSAIDs. Thrombotic events in aspirin users were consistent across all treatment groups and valdecoxib doses. Short- and intermediate-term use of valdecoxib at therapeutic (10 or 20 mg daily) and supratherapeutic (40 or 80 mg daily) doses did not show a higher risk of thrombotic events compared to nonselective NSAIDs or placebo in arthritis patients.

title: Identification of a Novel WFS1 Mutation in Japanese Patients with Wolfram Syndrome
abstract: A novel WFS1 mutation (AFF344 - 345ins) was identified in Japanese patients with Wolfram syndrome. Wolfram syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by early onset diabetes mellitus, optic atrophy, sensorineural deafness, and diabetes insipidus. Affected individuals may also exhibit renal tract abnormalities, neurologic issues, and psychiatric syndromes. The WFS1 gene, which encodes a transmembrane protein, was confirmed as the causative factor for this condition. This study reports a Japanese family where two members presented with Wolfram syndrome. In the WFS1 gene of these patients, a nine nucleotide insertion (nine nucleotide insertion) was detected. Additionally, one patient showed preclinical hypopituitarism, an uncommon feature of Wolfram syndrome. Since only the two family members homozygous for the mutation exhibited the syndrome, these findings support the role of this mutation in causing Wolfram syndrome.

title: Genetic Investigation of Serotonergic Enzymes in Migraine and Headache Disorders
abstract: A genome-wide analysis of serotonergic biosynthetic pathways in migraine patients revealed key enzymatic roles in headache disorders. Migraine, a common primary headache disorder, is associated with altered brain neurotransmitter function, including 5-hydroxytryptamine (5-HT), which plays a critical role in pain signaling. This study examined genetic variants in tryptophan hydroxylase (TPH), amino acid decarboxylase (AADC), and monoamine oxidase A (MAOA) genes, which are central to serotonin metabolism. Using a DNA pooling strategy, researchers evaluated single nucleotide polymorphisms and other genetic markers across these loci. While the study identified no significant associations between MAOA, TPH, or AADC variants and migraine susceptibility, it confirmed the positive correlation between 5-hydroxytryptamine levels and migraine frequency. Neurotransmitter dynamics in headache disorders were further analyzed, highlighting the complex interplay between serotonergic enzymes and neurochemical balance.

title: S-1 and 5-Fluorouracil-Induced Cardiotoxicity in Patients with Malignancies
abstract: A 65-year-old woman with metastatic colon cancer and 5-Fluorouracil-induced cardiotoxicity was evaluated for treatment adjustments. During therapy, high serum levels of alpha-fluoro-beta-alanine were detected, correlating with cardiac symptoms including precordial pain and right bundle branch block. The patient, who had unresectable malignancies, experienced severe cardiac manifestations following 5-Fluorouracil administration. After discontinuation of 5-Fluorouracil, symptoms resolved spontaneously. S-1, a derivative of 5-Fluorouracil, was initiated due to its inhibitory effect on dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase, which reduces alpha-fluoro-beta-alanine production. Serum alpha-fluoro-beta-alanine levels decreased to baseline, and no cardiac symptoms recurred. The patient achieved partial response after 6 months of S-1 treatment. This case highlights the relationship between alpha-fluoro-beta-alanine and 5-Fluorouracil-induced cardiotoxicity, suggesting S-1 may be a safer alternative in patients with cardiotoxicity. Additional indexed biomedical mentions considered for relation extraction included: metastases.

title: Pilocarpine's Impact on Auditory Discrimination and Seizures in Animal Models
abstract: Pilocarpine administration is associated with impairment in auditory location discrimination, as demonstrated in experimental models. Animals exposed to pilocarpine exhibit status epilepticus, a condition linked to seizures and long-term auditory deficits. The relationship between pilocarpine and these phenotypic features highlights a positive correlation in disease progression. Studies using a rat model revealed that pilocarpine-induced status epilepticus at specific developmental stages correlates with severe auditory discrimination impairments, while seizures are a key manifestation of this condition. These findings underscore the complex interplay between pilocarpine, status epilepticus, and auditory deficits in neurological outcomes.

title: Genetic Variants in PTPN22 and Their Association with Autoimmune Conditions in Caucasian Populations
abstract: This study investigates the role of three polymorphisms in the PTPN22 gene—-1123 G > C (rs2488457), + 1858C > T (rs2476601), and and+2740 A > G (rs1217412)—in relation to autoimmune diseases and type 1 diabetes in two Caucasian populations. The PTPN22 gene, which regulates T cell activity, has been linked to multiple autoimmune conditions, including juvenile idiopathic arthritis and type 1 diabetes. The -1123 G > C variant was previously associated with susceptibility, but this analysis explores its independent contribution. In the Czech population, all three SNPs showed strong linkage disequilibrium, while in the Azeri population, only the -1123 and +2740 variants were in strong linkage. Haplotype analysis revealed that the minor allele at codon 620 (R620W) was significantly associated with type 1 diabetes and juvenile idiopathic arthritis. However, the -1123 and +2740 variants did not independently contribute to autoimmune risk. Autoimmune diseases were found to be associated with PTPN22 polymorphisms, but the + 1858C > T variant showed a positive correlation with type 1 diabetes. These findings indicate that while the -1123 and +2740 SNPs do not independently influence autoimmune conditions, the R620W substitution in PTPN22 remains a critical factor in susceptibility.

title: Effect of Delayed Hypertension on Brain Edema After Cerebral Ischemia
abstract: Delayed induction of hypertension following focal cerebral ischemia was examined for its impact on brain edema and neuronal injury. In a study involving 14 spontaneously hypertensive rats, middle cerebral artery occlusion (MCAO) was performed, followed by a 2-hour delay before initiating hypertension. The control group (n=7) maintained normal mean arterial pressure (MAP), while the hypertensive group (n=7) experienced a 25-30 mm Hg elevation in MAP starting 2 hours post-MCAO. Four hours after MCAO, brains were harvested and sectioned to assess subcortical and cortical regions. Specific gravity (SG) measurements revealed reduced edema accumulation in the cortical periphery of the hypertensive group compared to controls (1.041 ± 0.001 vs 1.039 ± 0.001, P < 0.05). Neuronal injury was evaluated using 2,3,5-triphenyltetrazolium staining, showing a 33% ± 3% reduction in injury area in the hypertensive group versus 21% ± 2% in controls. Phenylephrine-induced hypertension, when initiated 2 hours after MCAO, did not worsen ischemic core edema but improved peripheral edema and reduced neuronal dysfunction. Isoflurane was used for anesthesia during MCAO, and cerebral ischemia was monitored throughout the study. Brain edema and neuronal injury were consistently assessed in both groups, with hypertension showing a positive correlation with reduced neuronal injury.

title: Phosphatidylethanolamine N-Methyltransferase Polymorphism and NASH Susceptibility in Non-obese Individuals
abstract: A single nucleotide polymorphism in the phosphatidylethanolamine N-methyltransferase gene, V175 M, is associated with increased susceptibility to non-obese patients with non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH). The study examined the role of the Val175Met variant in the development of NASH, focusing on its relationship with phosphatidylethanolamine and phosphatidylcholine metabolism. Blood samples from 107 NASH patients and 150 healthy controls were analyzed for the presence of the Val175Met variant. The results showed a significantly higher frequency of the variant in NASH patients compared to controls. Additionally, non-obese individuals with the Val175Met variant were more likely to develop NASH than those without the variant. The study highlights the potential of the V175 M polymorphism as a biomarker for NASH susceptibility, particularly in non-obese populations. Phosphatidylethanolamine N-methyltransferase activity was found to influence the conversion of phosphatidylethanolamine to phosphatidylcholine, which may contribute to the pathogenesis of NASH.

title: Polymorphisms in Tenomodulin and Their Association with Obesity and Diabetes Risk: A Population-Based Study
abstract: Tenomodulin (64102) was found to be associated with obesity (D009765) and the risk of type 2 diabetes (D003924) in a recent study. The Finnish Diabetes Prevention Study (DPS) examined 507 participants and identified several single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) linked to adiposity, glucose metabolism, and diabetes risk. Seven SNPs from two haploblocks were analyzed, revealing sex-specific effects. rs5966709 and rs4828037 were associated with adiposity features in women, while rs11798018 showed similar associations in men. rs2073163 and rs1155794 correlated with 2-hour plasma glucose levels in men during a 3-year follow-up. These markers, along with rs2073162, were linked to the conversion of impaired glucose tolerance (D018149) to type 2 diabetes (D003924) in men. Higher 2-hour glucose levels were associated with an approximately 2-fold increased risk of developing diabetes, as evidenced by hazard ratios for rs2073162-A (2.192), rs2073163-C (2.191), and rs1155974-T (1.998). These findings suggest that Tenomodulin polymorphisms are connected to adiposity, glucose metabolism, and the progression from impaired glucose tolerance to type 2 diabetes in men. Additional indexed biomedical mentions considered for relation extraction included: rs1155974-T.; overweight.

title: Genetic Variants in Innate Immune Receptors and Their Association with Antibody Production in Inflammatory Bowel Disease
abstract: Mutations in pattern recognition receptor genes influence the development of antimicrobial antibodies in patients with inflammatory bowel disease. This study examines how genetic variations in innate immune receptors, including TLR2, TLR4, and NOD1/CARD4, affect antibody responses to microbial antigens. Patients with ulcerative colitis, Crohn's disease, and colitis were analyzed for anti-Saccharomyces cerevisiae antibodies (gASCA), anti-laminaribioside antibodies (ALCA), and other microbial epitope-specific antibodies. Variants in NOD2/CARD15, TLR1, TLR6, and TLR4 were associated with higher antibody positivity in Crohn's disease patients, particularly those carrying CARD15 mutations. Conversely, TLR4 D299 G and TLR2 P631H variants were linked to lower prevalence of certain antibodies, indicating a negative correlation. The study highlights the role of innate immune receptor diversity in shaping immune responses to intestinal bacteria, with implications for understanding the pathogenesis of inflammatory bowel disease. Additional indexed biomedical mentions considered for relation extraction included: Toll-like receptor ( TLR ) 4; Crohn 's disease.

title: Genetic Analysis of Meiotic Genes in Patients with Infertility and Premature Ovarian Failure
abstract: This study investigates the association between mutations in meiotic genes and reproductive disorders, focusing on infertility and premature ovarian failure. A case-control design was employed to examine the prevalence of specific genetic variants in patients with these conditions. Genomic DNA was sequenced from 41 individuals diagnosed with premature ovarian failure and 36 fertile controls. Analysis revealed a heterozygous missense mutation in the MSH5 gene, involving a cytosine residue substitution with thymidine at exon 2, which was observed in two Caucasian patients. This mutation alters a non-polar proline to a polar serine at position 29 (P29S). No similar mutation was detected in controls or other POF patients. Additionally, a homozygous nucleotide change in the DMC1 gene, leading to the M200V substitution, was identified in an African-origin patient with POF. These findings support the role of meiotic gene mutations in the pathogenesis of infertility and premature ovarian failure. The study underscores the potential of MSH5 and DMC1 mutations as genetic contributors to these conditions, although their prevalence remains low. Additional indexed biomedical mentions considered for relation extraction included: SPO11; MSH4; cytosine residue with thymidine; MutS.

title: Genetic Variants and Autoimmune Disease Susceptibility: A Study on IRF5 and Related Factors
abstract: A single nucleotide polymorphism in the IRF5 promoter region is linked to susceptibility to autoimmune diseases, particularly rheumatoid arthritis. Interferon regulatory factor 5 (IRF5) plays a critical role in regulating proinflammatory cytokines, which are central to the pathogenesis of systemic lupus erythaematosus and other inflammatory conditions. Polymorphisms in the IRF5 gene have been associated with increased risk of rheumatoid arthritis in Japanese populations, as well as with systemic lupus erythaematosus in Caucasian and Asian groups. This study evaluated the genetic role of IRF5 in autoimmune diseases, focusing on its interaction with leukocyte antigen (HLA)-DRB1. Case-control analyses revealed a significant association between the rs729302 A allele and rheumatoid arthritis susceptibility. When stratified by HLA-DRB1 shared epitope status, the rs729302 A allele showed a stronger risk in SE-negative patients. While no other polymorphisms reached statistical significance, the rs729302 variant remained a key genetic factor. These findings highlight the involvement of IRF5 in autoimmune disease pathogenesis, particularly in individuals with specific HLA-DRB1 profiles.

title: Spectral Analysis of Penicillin-Induced Epileptiform Activity in Rats
abstract: This study investigates the spectral characteristics of penicillin-induced epileptiform activity in anesthetized rats. The penicillin model remains a standard tool for epilepsy research, and this work aims to characterize the electrical activity changes induced by penicillin. Rats were anesthetized with urethane and monitored for electrocorticogram activity. Following baseline recordings, penicillin-G potassium was administered to induce epileptiform activity, which was then compared to control periods. Spectral analysis revealed significant changes in delta, theta, beta-2, and gamma-2 bands during epileptiform episodes. The results demonstrate that penicillin-induced activity correlates with increased epileptiform activity, while urethane and penicillin-G potassium were used together without direct functional interaction. These findings provide insights into the mechanisms underlying experimental epilepsies.

title: Expanding Clinical Spectrum of Non-Autoimmune Hyperthyroidism Due to an Activating Germline Mutation in the Thyrotropin Receptor Gene
abstract: A novel germline mutation in the thyrotropin receptor gene, p. M453 T, is associated with a distinct clinical presentation of non-autoimmune hyperthyroidism. This study examines a family with three affected individuals, all exhibiting hyperthyroidism and ventriculomegaly. Genetic analysis revealed the mutation in the thyrotropin receptor gene, which is linked to the development of hyperthyroidism and ventriculomegaly. The mutation also correlates with the presence of bilateral shortening of the fifth metacarpal bones and middle phalanges of the fifth fingers. These findings highlight the expanded phenotypic features of non-autoimmune hyperthyroidism caused by this mutation, underscoring the importance of genetic testing in cases of hyperthyroidism with atypical presentations.

title: Hemodynamic and Autonomic Responses During Tilt Testing in Patients with Vasovagal Syncope: Association with Renin-Angiotensin and Serotonin System Polymorphisms
abstract: This study investigated the relationship between polymorphisms in the renin-angiotensin system and serotonin transporter genes with hemodynamic parameters and autonomic responses during postural testing in patients with vasovagal syncope. DNA was collected from 191 participants (mean age 44±18 years, 61 males, 130 females). Key polymorphisms analyzed included angiotensin-converting enzyme insertion/deletion (I/D ACE), angiotensinogen gene (M 235), angiotensin II receptor type 1 (A 11666C), and serotonin transporter (5HTTLPR). Heart rate variability was assessed during tilt testing using low frequency, high frequency, SDNN, and RMSSD measures. Results showed that the AA genotype of A 11666C was associated with lower minimal systolic and diastolic blood pressures during tilt, compared to other genotypes (P=0.007). Additionally, AA carriers exhibited higher SDNN values in early tilt phases and at syncope onset (P=0.01 and P=0.04, respectively). The A 11666C polymorphism in the angiotensin II receptor type 1 gene was linked to hypotension and reduced sympathetic activity during tilt testing. These findings suggest a potential genetic predisposition to vasovagal syncope through interactions with the renin-angiotensin and serotonin systems.

title: Genetic Polymorphisms and Clinical Features in Parkinson's Disease
abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD), a neurodegenerative disorder, is characterized by muscular rigidity, resting tremor, and bradykinesia. A study examined the role of the Serotonin transporter gene (SLC6A4) and its polymorphic region, the insertion/deletion (long allele-L/short allele-S) of 43 bp, in PD risk. The polymorphic element 5-HTTLPR was analyzed alongside the single nucleotide polymorphism rs25531(A-->G). Subjects included 837 individuals (393 PD cases, 444 controls). The 5-HTTLPR variant showed a positive correlation with PD risk, as indicated by an odds ratio of 1.7 (95% CI 1.2-2.5, p=0.002). However, rs25531 and its haplotype did not associate with PD. The study highlights the potential of the 5-HTTLPR polymorphic element in modulating genetic susceptibility to PD in the studied population. Additional indexed biomedical mentions considered for relation extraction included: insertion/deletion ( long allele-L/short allele-S ) of 43 bp; Parkinson 's disease.

title: Therapeutic Hypothermia in Acetaminophen-Induced Fulminant Hepatic Failure and Cerebral Edema
abstract: Prolonged therapeutic hypothermia was employed as a critical intervention for cerebral edema and intracranial hypertension associated with fulminant hepatic failure. This case report examines the use of hypothermia in a 28-year-old male with acetaminophen overdose leading to fulminant hepatic failure and resultant cerebral edema. The patient presented with depressed mental status and signs of toxicity following acetaminophen ingestion over 3 days. Initial assessment confirmed fulminant hepatic failure from acetaminophen and cerebral edema. Treatment included hyperosmolar therapy, hyperventilation, sedation, and paralysis. Despite maximal medical management, intracranial pressure remained elevated. Therapeutic hypothermia was initiated and maintained for 6 days, leading to resolution of cerebral edema and intracranial hypertension. Post-rewarming, the patient achieved neurological and hepatic recovery. This case suggests that prolonged hypothermia may serve as a bridge to recovery in acetaminophen-induced fulminant hepatic failure with cerebral edema, highlighting its potential as a life-saving therapy.

title: hOGG1 Ser326Cys Polymorphism and Risk of Lung Cancer by Histological Subtype
abstract: The hOGG1 Ser326Cys polymorphism influences the repair of 8-hydroxyguanine, a key DNA lesion involved in cancer development. This genetic variation, defined by the rs1052133 marker, leads to reduced enzymatic activity in the Cys326 variant. Studies have explored its link to lung cancer risk, but the impact on specific histological subtypes remains under investigation. A case-control study involving 515 lung cancer patients and 1030 control subjects without cancer revealed that the Cys/Cys genotype was significantly associated with lung cancer compared to the Ser allele. Histological analysis showed a strong positive correlation between the Cys/Cys genotype and small-cell carcinoma, with a marginally significant association with adenocarcinoma. Meta-analysis of existing and new data confirmed a positive relationship with adenocarcinoma, while suggestive links were observed for squamous- and small-cell lung cancers. These findings highlight the role of rs1052133 in contributing to the risk of adenocarcinoma of lung.

title: CCL2 and CCR2 Expression in Hippocampal Neuroinflammation Following Pilocarpine-Induced Seizures
abstract: Chemokine CCL2 and its receptor CCR2 are elevated in the hippocampus after pilocarpine-induced status epilepticus. Neuroinflammation is a key feature following seizures and is linked to epileptogenesis. CCR2 functions as a receptor for CCL2, and their interaction promotes monocyte infiltration in neuroinflammatory processes. In this study, CCR2 and CCL2 expression were assessed after status epilepticus (SE) induced by pilocarpine injection. Control rats received saline instead of pilocarpine. Five days post-SE, CCR2 staining in neurons and glial cells was analyzed using immunohistochemical methods. The number of CCR2-positive cells was quantified with stereology in the hippocampus. CCL2 expression in the hippocampus was evaluated via molecular assays. Results showed increased CCR2 levels in the hippocampus after SE. Seizures also altered the cell types expressing CCR2. More neurons expressed CCR2 following SE. Microglial cells were closer to CCR2-labeled cells in SE rats. Additionally, SE rats exhibited CCR2 labeling in hypertrophied astrocytes, particularly in CA1 and dentate gyrus. These CCR2+ astrocytes were absent in control rats. CCL2 expression was elevated in the hippocampus after SE. The findings indicate that CCR2 and CCL2 are up-regulated in the hippocampus following pilocarpine-induced SE. Seizures also induce changes in CCR2 receptor expression in neurons and astrocytes. These changes may contribute to neuroplasticity and neuroinflammatory processes after seizures.

title: Gene Expression Profiles in Adipose Tissues of Obese Individuals: Insights into Lipid Metabolism and Inflammatory Responses
abstract: Obesity is increasingly prevalent, with significant variation in metabolic outcomes among affected individuals. This study examines gene expression patterns in subcutaneous and omental adipose tissues from morbidly obese subjects, categorizing them based on plasma levels of adipocyte-specific protein (ASP) and triglyceride (TG). Participants were divided into Low Acylation Stimulating Protein (ASP) and Triglyceride (TG) (LAT) versus High ASP and TG (HAT) groups. Microarray analysis of adipose tissues revealed distinct gene expression profiles, with HAT samples showing increased expression of lipid storage-related genes including DGAT1, DGAT2, FASN, SCD1, CD36, and LPL. Conversely, genes involved in lipolysis, such as HSL, CES1, and perilipin, were downregulated. Inflammatory markers like MMP2, PIG7, and TIMP1, TIMP3, TIMP4 were elevated in HAT, while anti-inflammatory genes such as TGFB1, UCP1, and CPT1 were reduced. The upregulation of C5L2, an ASP receptor, suggests a compensatory pathway associated with increased TG storage. These findings highlight the complex interplay between lipid metabolism, inflammation, and ASP expression in obese individuals, providing insights into potential therapeutic targets for metabolic disorders. Additional indexed biomedical mentions considered for relation extraction included: fatty acid binding proteins; glucose; adipsin; IRS-1; InsR; CEBPbeta; factor B; insulin; CEBPalpha; AMPK; insulin resistance; PPARgamma; FABP7; adipokine.

title: A Case of GH Insensitivity Syndrome with Insulin-like Growth Factor-I Deficiency and Genetic Mutations in the GH Receptor
abstract: A 5-year-old boy presents with GH insensitivity syndrome and insulin-like growth factor-I deficiency. Despite normal serum GH-binding protein levels, he exhibits growth failure and elevated GH concentrations. Genetic analysis reveals compound heterozygous mutations in the GH receptor, including R211H and a novel 899dupC mutation, leading to a frameshift and premature stop codon. Serum IGF-I and IGFBP-3 levels are abnormally low. Treatment with recombinant IGF-I results in growth acceleration. These findings highlight the role of intracellular GH receptor mutations in causing GH insensitivity and IGF deficiency, even with normal GHBP.

title: Genetic Polymorphisms and Hypertension Risk in Patients with Aldosterone-Producing Adenomas
abstract: This study investigates the relationship between DNA polymorphisms in the CYP11B2/CYP11B1 locus and postoperative hypertension outcomes in patients with aldosterone-producing adenomas. Hypertension often persists following adrenalectomy for primary aldosteronism, and genetic factors may play a role in this condition. The research evaluated the association between rs1799998, rs4539, rs6387, rs6410, and the development of persistent hypertension after surgical removal of aldosterone-producing adenomas. Patients were analyzed for genetic variants within steroid synthesis genes, including CYP11B2 and CYP11B1, which are critical for aldosterone production. Results showed that hypertension was positively correlated with rs4539 and rs1799998, while aldosterone-producing adenomas were associated with rs6387 and rs6410. Multivariate analysis revealed that specific haplotypes, such as H1, H2, and H3, were linked to persistent hypertension, highlighting the genetic susceptibility of certain populations. Other risk factors, including prolonged hypertension duration and family history, also contributed to postoperative hypertension. These findings suggest that genetic polymorphisms in the CYP11B2/CYP11B1 region may influence hypertension outcomes in patients with aldosterone-producing adenomas.

title: A Novel Mutation in GJA8 Associated with Cataract-Microcornea Syndrome
abstract: A novel mutation in GJA8, c.592C-->T, was identified in a family with cataract-microcornea syndrome, which is associated with a genetic defect. The study aimed to determine the underlying genetic cause in a family of Japanese descent with autosomal dominant cataract-microcornea syndrome. Genomic DNA was extracted from peripheral blood, and candidate genes were sequenced. Results showed a heterozygous mutation in exon 2 of GJA8, leading to a substitution of arginine to tryptophan at codon 198 (p.R198W). This mutation co-segregates with affected members but was not found in non-carriers or 100 normal controls. The findings confirm the role of GJA8 in cataract-microcornea syndrome, expanding the known mutations linked to congenital cataract and microcornea. The study highlights the gene's involvement in lens development and anterior segment structures.

title: The M235 T Polymorphism of the Angiotensinogen Gene in Patients with Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy
abstract: This study examines the relationship between the M235 T polymorphism of the angiotensinogen gene and various cardiac conditions, including left ventricular hypertrophy, hypertension, and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. A cohort of 150 patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (90 sporadic hypertrophic cardiomyopathy [SHCM] and 60 familial hypertrophic cardiomyopathy [FHCM]) was compared with 165 age- and sex-matched controls without known hypertension or left ventricular hypertrophy. DNA was isolated from peripheral leukocytes, and the M235 T mutation in the angiotensinogen gene was analyzed. Results showed significant differences in genotypic distribution and allelic frequency between SHCM patients and controls, but no association with FHCM. The angiotensinogen gene was found to be associated with SHCM but not with FHCM. Cardiac disease and hypertension were also evaluated as potential correlates in this population.

title: Genetic Polymorphism of IL-17F and Thrombocytopenic Phenotypes in Autoimmune Conditions
abstract: The rs763780 polymorphism in the IL-17F gene has been linked to thrombocytopenic states in patients with chronic immune thrombocytopenia. This study explored the association between autoimmune diseases and the rs763780 variant, which affects the amino acid sequence at position 161. A total of 102 individuals with chronic immune thrombocytopenia and 188 healthy controls were analyzed. Genotyping revealed that the rs763780 CC genotype was significantly less common in the patient group compared to controls. Additionally, the presence of the rs763780 T allele was correlated with more severe thrombocytopenic manifestations, including platelet counts below 10^9/L. The findings indicate that the rs763780 variant may contribute to the pathogenesis of thrombocytopenic conditions in autoimmune disease settings. Additional indexed biomedical mentions considered for relation extraction included: Interleukin-17F.

title: XRCC1 Arg399Gln Polymorphism and Systemic Lupus Erythematosus Risk in a Polish Cohort
abstract: The XRCC1 Arg399Gln (rs25487) gene variant was evaluated for its association with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) in a Polish population. Analysis of 265 SLE patients and 360 controls revealed a statistically significant increased risk for the Gln/Gln genotype, with an odds ratio (OR) of 1.553 (95% CI=0.957-2.520, p=0.0729). The Gln allele showed an OR of 1.406 (95% CI=1.111-1.779, p=0.0045) for SLE susceptibility. Additionally, the Arg399Gln variant was positively correlated with malar rash (OR=2.241, 95% CI=1.328-3.781, p=0.0023) and photosensitivity in SLE patients. XRCC1 and Arg399Gln were found to have no direct biological relationship in this study, though both were associated with SLE progression. Meta-analyses across multiple populations confirmed the variant's role in SLE incidence, with ORs of 1.440 (95% CI=1.15-1.80, p=0.0019) for the Gln/Gln or Gln/Arg genotype and 1.27 (95% CI=1.08-1.51, p=0.0051) for the Gln allele.

title: Characterization of EPO/EPOR-Regulated Gene Expression in Erythropoiesis
abstract: This study investigates the EPOR-regulated transcriptome in primary progenitors, revealing Tnfr-sf13c as a novel mediator of EPO-dependent erythroblast formation. Contrary to previous assumptions, in vivo studies show elevated Bcl-x levels in maturing erythroblasts but not in their progenitors. Truncated EPOR alleles, lacking a major p85/PI3 K recruitment site, promote polycythemia, while Erk1 disruption unexpectedly enhances erythropoiesis. Global transcriptome analyses of primary bone marrow-derived CFUe-like progenitors identified 160 EPO/EPOR target transcripts, with significant modulation ranging from 2-fold to 21.8-fold. A unique set of survival factors, including Lyl1, Gas5, Pim3, Pim1, Bim, Trib3, and Serpina 3 g., are regulated by EPO/EPOR. Cell cycle mediators such as Cdc25a, Btg3, Cyclin-d2, p27-kip1, Cyclin-g2, and CyclinB1-IP-1 are also modulated. Signal transduction factors like Socs3, Socs2, Spred2, Spred1, and Eaf1 are EPO-induced as negative-feedback components. Tnfr-sf13c, up-modulated >5-fold by EPO, promotes proerythroblast survival and enhances erythroblast formation. The EPOR engages a complex network of transcriptome response circuits, with Tnfr-sf13c acting as a novel positive regulator of proerythroblast formation. These findings highlight the intricate regulatory mechanisms involving EPO/EPOR and their implications in anemia and polycythemia. Additional indexed biomedical mentions considered for relation extraction included: EPOR/Jak2/Stat5; EPOR-; EPO-.

title: Genetic Variants of HOMER1 Gene Linked to Levodopa-Induced Adverse Effects in Parkinson's Disease
abstract: This study explores the association between common genetic variants of the HOMER1 gene and levodopa-related adverse effects in patients with Parkinson's disease. Levodopa remains the most effective symptomatic treatment for Parkinson's disease, yet its long-term use is associated with complications such as dyskinesia, visual hallucinations, and motor fluctuations. HOMER1, a protein critical for glutamate signaling, has been implicated in the pathogenesis of these complications. A cohort of 205 idiopathic Parkinson's disease patients was analyzed for polymorphisms in the HOMER1 gene promoter region, including rs4704559, rs10942891, and rs4704560. The rs4704559 G allele was found to be associated with a reduced prevalence of dyskinesia (prevalence ratio=0.615, 95% confidence interval=0.426-0.887, P=0.009) and visual hallucinations (prevalence ratio=0.515, 95% confidence interval=0.295-0.899, P=0.020). These findings suggest that the HOMER1 rs4704559 G allele may confer protection against levodopa-induced adverse effects. Additionally, the study highlights the potential role of rs10942891 and rs4704560 in modulating the risk of these complications, though no significant associations were observed for these specific variants. Additional indexed biomedical mentions considered for relation extraction included: Parkinson 's disease.

title: Serotonin and Methyldopa Effects on Hypotensive and Hypertensive Responses in Rat Models
abstract: Midline B3 serotonin nerves in rat medulla play a key role in the hypotensive effects of methyldopa. Studies have shown that microinjection of methyldopa into the ventrolateral region of B3 serotonin neurons in the medulla induces a hypotensive response through descending pathways to the spinal cord. This research examines the role of midline B3 serotonin neurons in the medulla, particularly in the raphe magnus, in both spontaneously hypertensive and stroke-prone rats. Microinjection of methyldopa into the midline B3 serotonin cell group in the ventral medulla caused a significant hypotension of 30-40 mm Hg, peaking 2-3 hours post-administration. This effect was blocked by intracerebroventricular injection of 5,7-dihydroxytryptamine (5,7-DHT), a serotonin neurotoxin. However, selective lesions of descending serotonin projections in the spinal cord did not affect the hypotension. Additionally, 5,7-DHT lesions of serotonin nerves in the median forebrain bundle, a major ascending pathway from B3 serotonin cells, did not alter the blood pressure response. These findings suggest that midline B3 serotonin cells in the medulla contribute to methyldopa-induced hypotension via an ascending pathway not involving the median forebrain bundle or through restricted caudal brainstem projections. Serotonin's association with hypotensive responses is well established, while its relation to hypertensive states remains unclear. Methyldopa and serotonin exhibit a positive correlation in hypotensive effects, whereas no direct relation exists between serotonin and hypertensive conditions. 5,7-Dihydroxytryptamine and methyldopa show no direct association with stroke-prone phenotypes.

title: NADPH oxidase 4 and VEGF receptor 2 in retinopathy of prematurity
abstract: NADPH oxidase 4 mediates vascular endothelial growth factor receptor 2-induced intravitreal neovascularization in a rat model of retinopathy of prematurity. NADPH oxidase-generated reactive oxygen species are involved in angiogenesis. NOX4 is the most prevalent isoform of NADPH oxidase in vascular endothelial cells. In oxygen-induced retinopathy, NOX4 expression decreases during development and increases at postnatal day 18. Retinal cryosections show increased colabeling of NOX4 with lectin-stained endothelial cells in OIR compared to room air. VEGF induces ROS generation and activates VEGFR2 and STAT3 in endothelial cells. Knockdown of NOX4 reduces VEGF-induced ROS and inhibits VEGFR2 activation, but does not abolish it. NOX4 deficiency also prevents STAT3 activation in response to VEGF. VEGF-stimulated endothelial cell proliferation is inhibited by NOX4 or STAT3 knockdown. These findings suggest that NOX4 regulates VEGFR2-mediated neovascularization through STAT3 activation in retinopathy of prematurity. Additional indexed biomedical mentions considered for relation extraction included: VEGF receptor 2.

title: Role of Endodermal b-Catenin Signaling in Anorectal Malformations
abstract: Disruption of temporally regulated cloaca endodermal b-catenin signaling leads to anorectal malformations. The cloaca forms temporally and is divided by the urorectal septum (URS) during urogenital and anorectal organ development. Congenital malformations, such as anorectal malformations (ARMs), are frequently observed in this process, but underlying mechanisms remain unclear. b-Catenin is critical for canonical Wnt signaling and regulates cell differentiation during embryogenesis. Its expression is observed in endodermal epithelia, including URS epithelia. We modulated b-catenin gene expression in endodermal epithelia using tamoxifen-inducible Cre driver (Shh(CreERT2). Both b-catenin loss- and gain-of-function mutants exhibited abnormal perineal clefts and hypoplastic URS elongation. Mutants also showed reduced proliferation in URS mesenchyme. B-catenin gain-of-function mutants displayed decreased apoptosis and increased apoptosis in URS epithelium, leading to reduced differentiation markers like keratin 1 and filaggrin. Ectopic induction of bone morphogenetic protein (Bmp) genes, such as Bmp4 and Bmp7, was observed in URS epithelia. Msx2 gene and phosphorylated-Smad1/5/8 expression were increased in mutants. Additionally, BmprIA mutation partially restored URS elongation. These results indicate that ARM phenotypes in b-catenin gain-of-function mutants result from abnormal Bmp signaling. This analysis highlights the close relationship between endodermal b-catenin signaling and ARM phenotypes. Additional indexed biomedical mentions considered for relation extraction included: Bmp receptor.

title: Evaluating the Anticonvulsant Effects of Garcinielliptone FC in Pilocarpine-Induced Seizures
abstract: This study investigates the anticonvulsant potential of garcinielliptone FC (GFC) in mice subjected to pilocarpine-induced seizures. GFC, derived from the hexanic fraction of Platonia insignis seed extract, is traditionally used to treat skin diseases and diarrheas in both humans and animals. The research assesses GFC's impact at doses of 25, 50, and 75 mg/kg on seizure parameters, focusing on its effects on amino acid levels (r-aminobutyric acid, glutamine, aspartate, and glutathione) and acetylcholinesterase (AChE) activity in the hippocampus following seizures. GFC treatment significantly increased the latency to the first seizure, with 75 mg/kg demonstrating the highest effect. Additionally, GFC75 combined with P400 elevated hippocampal GABA levels by 46.90% compared to control groups. In contrast, aspartate, glutamine, and glutamate levels decreased by 5.21%, 13.55%, and 21.80%, respectively. AChE activity was notably increased by 63.30% in GFC75-treated mice. These findings suggest that GFC exerts anticonvulsant activity by modulating GABA and glutamate levels and AChE function, potentially reducing the frequency of pilocarpine-induced status epilepticus. The results highlight GFC's potential as a therapeutic agent for epilepsy through its influence on neurotransmitter dynamics and neuronal protection. Additional indexed biomedical mentions considered for relation extraction included: inflammatory diseases.

title: Sirolimus Mitigates Cyclosporine-Induced Nephropathy: Biomarker Analysis in Renal Tissue and Serum
abstract: Conversion to sirolimus ameliorates cyclosporine-induced nephropathy in the rat : focus on serum, urine, gene, and protein renal expression biomarkers. Protocols of conversion from cyclosporin A (CsA) to sirolimus (SRL) have been widely used in immunotherapy after transplantation to prevent CsA-induced nephropathy, but the molecular mechanisms underlying these protocols remain unclear. This study aimed to identify the molecular pathways and putative biomarkers of CsA-to-SRL conversion in a rat model. Four animal groups (n = 6) were tested during 9 weeks: control, CsA, SRL, and conversion (CsA for 3 weeks followed by SRL for 6 weeks). Classical and emergent serum, urinary, and kidney tissue (gene and protein expression) markers were assessed. Renal lesions were analyzed in hematoxylin and eosin, periodic acid-Schiff, and Masson's trichrome stains. SRL-treated rats presented proteinuria and NGAL (serum and urinary) as the best markers of renal impairment. Short CsA treatment presented slight or even absent kidney lesions and TGF-b, NF-kb, mTOR, PCNA, TP53, KIM-1, and CTGF as relevant gene and protein changes. Prolonged CsA exposure aggravated renal damage, without clear changes on the traditional markers, but with changes in serum TGF-b and IL-7, TBARs clearance, and kidney TGF-b and mTOR. Conversion to SRL prevented CsA-induced renal damage evolution (absent/mild grade lesions), while NGAL (serum versus urine) seems to be a feasible biomarker of CsA replacement to SRL. sirolimus treatment was associated with decreased TBARs levels, and cyclosporine-induced nephropathy was correlated with increased NF-kb activity. TGF-b expression was positively correlated with mTOR activation, and sirolimus treatment led to reduced TP53 expression. Proteinuria was associated with increased KIM-1 and CTGF levels, while NGAL levels were negatively correlated with renal damage severity. Cyclosporine-induced TBARs formation was compared to sirolimus-induced oxidative stress markers, and TGF-b was found to be associated with IL-7 production. mTOR and PCNA levels were found to be negatively correlated in renal tissue, and sirolimus treatment was associated with reduced NF-kb activity. NGAL expression was associated with proteinuria, and TGF-b was associated with increased mTOR expression. KIM-1 levels were positively correlated with cyclosporine-induced nephropathy, and TP53 was found to be associated with PCNA expression. CTGF and IL-7 levels were found to be positively correlated, and NGAL was associated with reduced nephropathy severity. TGF-b was found to be associated with increased NF-kb activity, and sirolimus treatment was associated with reduced TBARs levels. Proteinuria was associated with increased KIM-1 and CTGF levels, while NGAL levels were negatively correlated with renal damage severity. Additional indexed biomedical mentions considered for relation extraction included: NF- kb.

title: Characterization of a Novel BCHE Allele with Altered Functionality
abstract: A novel BCHE variant, c.695T > A (p. Val204Asp), was identified in a patient exhibiting prolonged neuromuscular block and apnea following suxamethonium administration. This mutation, associated with Butyrylcholinesterase deficiency, leads to reduced enzymatic activity and impaired substrate binding. Analysis of butyrylthiocholine and benzoylcholine inhibition revealed altered kinetic parameters, with Km values significantly elevated compared to atypical variants. The patient's plasma showed decreased tetrameric BCHE levels, alongside the absence of minor fast-moving BChE components. Molecular dynamics simulations indicated disruption of hydrogen bonding critical for catalytic triad function, contributing to the 'silent' phenotype. Dibucaine and fluoride binding studies aligned with heterozygous atypical genotype, while mivacurium administration correlated with prolonged neuromuscular block. The variant p. Val204Asp/p . Asp70Gly-p . Ala539Thr was found to display pure Michaelian behavior with BTC as substrate, reflecting reduced activity against suxamethonium. This case highlights the role of BCHE mutations in modulating neuromuscular block and apnea, underscoring the importance of genetic screening in clinical settings. Additional indexed biomedical mentions considered for relation extraction included: p. Ala204Asp/p.

title: LDHA Inhibition Modulates Metabolic Pathways in Prostate Cancer
abstract: Inhibition of LDHA suppresses tumor progression in prostate cancer. A key hallmark of cancer cells is their altered metabolism, known as Warburg effect. Lactate dehydrogenase A (LDHA) executes the final step of aerobic glycolysis and has been reported to be involved in the tumor progression. However, the function of LDHA in prostate cancer has not been studied. In the current study, we observed overexpression of LDHA in clinical prostate cancer samples compared with benign prostate hyperplasia tissues as demonstrated by immunohistochemistry and real-time qPCR. Attenuated expression of LDHA by siRNA or inhibition of LDHA activities by FX11 inhibited cell proliferation, migration, invasion, and promoted cell apoptosis of PC-3 and DU145 cells. Mechanistically, decreased Warburg effect as demonstrated by reduced glucose consumption and lactate secretion and reduced expression of MMP-9, PLAU, and cathepsin B were found after LDHA knockdown or FX11 treatment in PC-3 and DU145 cells. Taken together, our study revealed the oncogenic role of LDHA in prostate cancer and suggested that LDHA might be a potential therapeutic target. Additionally, the study found that FX11 treatment led to a significant decrease in lactate levels, which was associated with reduced tumor size. Moreover, the correlation between glucose metabolism and lactate production was maintained, with lactate levels inversely related to the expression of cathepsin B. The findings indicate that the interplay between LDHA, lactate, and MMP-9 plays a critical role in the progression of prostate cancer and benign prostate hyperplasia.

title: The Role of Type I Interferon Receptor in Virus-Induced Autoimmune Diabetes
abstract: The Type I Interferon Receptor plays a critical role in the development of autoimmune diabetes following viral infection in rodents. Polyinosinic : polycytidylic acid, a viral mimic, induces diabetes in rats through mechanisms involving the Type I Interferon Receptor. Insulin-producing cells are targets of immune-mediated damage in Autoimmune Diabetes, while insulitis, a hallmark of this condition, is influenced by Type I Interferon Receptor activity. Diabetes is associated with the Type I Interferon Receptor, and polyinosinic : polycytidylic acid is positively correlated with Diabetes. The IFN receptor-mediated signaling pathways are essential in linking viral infection to immune-mediated pancreatic damage, highlighting the importance of innate immunity in autoimmune disease progression.

title: Genetic Variants in Sulfonylurea Receptor, Type 2 Diabetes, and Coronary Heart Disease
abstract: Genetic variations in the Sulfonylurea Receptor, Type 2 Diabetes, and Coronary Heart Disease were analyzed to explore their interrelationships. Despite its widespread use in managing Type 2 Diabetes, the long-term impact of sulfonylurea on cardiovascular health remains unclear. A common polymorphism in the ABCC8 gene (p. A1369S) influences the function of the Sulfonylurea Receptor, affecting insulin secretion. Using data from 120,286 participants in the UK Biobank and results from four large-scale genome-wide association studies, we examined how this variant interacts with metabolic traits. The p. A1369S variant was linked to a reduced risk of Type 2 Diabetes (odds ratio 0.93; 95% CI 0.91, 0.95; P = 1.2 x 10(-11)) and a lower risk of Coronary Heart Disease (odds ratio 0.98; 95% CI 0.96, 0.99; P = 5.9 x 10(-4)). It was also associated with increased body mass index (BMI) but a decreased waist-to-hip ratio. These findings suggest that while the variant may contribute to weight gain, it could potentially lower the risk of Coronary Heart Disease through its effects on insulin secretion.

title: Pituitary Response to LH-RH in Haloperidol-Induced Hyperprolactinemia
abstract: This study investigates the pituitary response to luteinizing hormone-releasing hormone (LH-RH) in patients with haloperidol-induced hyperprolactinemia. A 6-hour infusion of haloperidol was administered to male subjects, with serum prolactin and luteinizing hormone (LH) levels measured. Control subjects received 0.9% NaCl solution. Five hours post-infusion, the pituitary response to LH-RH was assessed. Haloperidol treatment resulted in significant hyperprolactinemia and abolished pituitary response to LH-RH compared to controls. NaCl administration did not alter prolactin or LH levels. The association between haloperidol-induced hyperprolactinemia and luteinizing hormone-releasing hormone was observed, along with a positive correlation between haloperidol-induced effects and hyperprolactinemia.

title: Molecular Analysis of VLCAD Deficiency and Its Association with Long-Chain Fatty Acids
abstract: The study characterized the molecular basis of VLCAD deficiency and its relationship with long-chain fatty acids. Mutant VLCAD-deficient patients were analyzed for genetic alterations, revealing a 105-bp deletion encompassing bases 1078-1182 in the very-long-chain acyl-coenzyme A dehydrogenase gene. This deletion was found to disrupt the normal function of the enzyme, leading to impaired metabolic processes. Long-chain fatty acid metabolism was assessed in patient-derived fibroblasts, showing a negative correlation with VLCAD activity. Palmitic acid, a key fatty acid, was identified as a critical component in the metabolic pathway affected by the deficiency. The study also noted a positive correlation between palmitic acid and the presence of the 105-bp deletion, suggesting a potential link between genetic mutations and fatty acid metabolism. Additionally, long-chain fatty acid and palmitic acid were observed to have no direct relation in this context, highlighting the complexity of fatty acid metabolism in VLCAD-deficient individuals. Additional indexed biomedical mentions considered for relation extraction included: 105-bp deletion encompassing bases 1078 - 1182.

title: Characterization of Human Opioid Peptides and Mu Opiate Receptor Interactions
abstract: A human mu opiate receptor (h mu OR1) has been cloned and characterized from a cerebral cortical cDNA library using sequences derived from the rat mu opiate receptor. The h mu OR1 exhibits 95% amino acid identity with the rat counterpart. Opioid peptides and tested opiate drugs bind to the receptor in a sodium- and GTP-sensitive manner, displaying affinities comparable to those observed in the rat receptor. The receptor's effects on cyclic AMP production mirror those of the rat counterpart. A 18 kb genomic clone hybridizing with the h mu OR1 cDNA contains exonic sequences of 63 and 489 bp, flanked by splice donor/acceptor regions. Chromosomal localization to 6q24-25 was confirmed through hybridization studies with human rodent hybrid cell lines and in situ hybridization. The receptor's involvement in neuropsychiatric disorders may be assessed via an MspI polymorphism that generates a 3.7 kb band.

title: Association of Adrenoleukodystrophy Gene with X-linked Adrenoleukodystrophy
abstract: The Adrenoleukodystrophy gene encodes a 80 kDa membrane-associated protein. A monoclonal antibody directed against the C-terminal region of this protein, derived from the gene responsible for X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy (ALD), was generated to identify the gene's product. The antibody recognized the 80 kDa band in normal fibroblasts but did not detect any protein bands in fibroblasts from a patient with ALD (#163), where mRNA levels of the ALD gene were not detectable by Northern blot. Transfection of 293 T cells with the full-length cDNA produced the 80 kDa protein, confirmed by Western blot. Immunocytochemical analysis revealed punctate staining in normal cells, absent in #163 cells. These findings support that the ALD gene codes for the 80 kDa membrane protein.

title: Genetic Variants and Clinical Phenotypes in Cerebellar Ataxia and Ataxia-Telangiectasia
abstract: This study explores the genetic basis of cerebellar ataxia and its relationship with ataxia-telangiectasia. We identified 14 families with ataxia-telangiectasia (A-T) where mutations in the ATM gene are linked to a milder clinical presentation. In 10 of these families, all homozygotes exhibit a 137-bp insertion in their cDNA due to a point mutation near a splice-donor site. The second A-T allele varies among patients, with some showing partial splicing from the insertion-containing allele. Patients with the lowest levels of the 137-bp PCR product experienced a later onset of cerebellar ataxia. Additionally, four families without the insertion were found, with two exhibiting missense mutations typically rare in A-T. These findings suggest that milder ATM mutations may contribute to a broader spectrum of phenotypes, raising questions about the prevalence of compound heterozygotes in A-T patients.

title: Role of Myotonic Dystrophy Protein Kinase in Ion Homeostasis
abstract: Myotonic dystrophy protein kinase plays a crucial role in maintaining Ca2+ homeostasis in skeletal muscle cells. Myotonic dystrophy, a prevalent muscular disorder, is associated with mutations in the gene encoding Myotonic dystrophy protein kinase. This study investigated the effects of DMPK deficiency on ion homeostasis in cultured skeletal muscle cells. In DMPK knockout mice, resting Ca2+ levels were elevated due to altered channel activity. Acetylcholine-induced Ca2+ transients were reduced, and ATP-driven ion pumps showed no significant changes. However, the presence of Na+ and K+ ions was found to influence these responses. Sarcoplasmic reticulum Ca2+ -ATPase activity remained unaffected, while the association between Myotonic dystrophy and the protein kinase was noted. These findings highlight the importance of DMPK in modulating ion balance, linking muscular disorder to Ca2+ dynamics. Additional indexed biomedical mentions considered for relation extraction included: Na +; Ca2 +; K +; sarcoplasmic reticulum Ca2 + -ATPase.

title: Antiepileptic Drug Efficacy and Safety in Pediatric Absence Seizures
abstract: Carbamazepine and vigabatrin are not recommended for treating typical absence seizures in children. Among 15 consecutive patients with refractory typical absences, six were incorrectly prescribed carbamazepine, either as monotherapy or as an adjunct. Vigabatrin was also administered to three patients. Increased seizure frequency was observed in four individuals taking carbamazepine, with two developing myoclonic jerks that resolved upon discontinuation. Seizures worsened in both cases where vigabatrin was added to existing therapies. Sodium valproate, lamotrigine, or ethosuximide were effective in controlling absences, either alone or in combination. Myoclonic jerks were not associated with any of these agents, and absence seizures were well-managed with these medications.

title: Genetic Variants in FCGR2B and CD72 Modulate Susceptibility to Systemic Lupus Erythematosus and Nephritis
abstract: Polymorphisms in CD72, an inhibitory B-cell receptor, were evaluated for their role in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and nephritis. This study identified FCGR2B-Ile232Thr as a variant associated with SLE in multiple populations. CD72 variants were linked to SLE in murine models and human cohorts. Analysis of Japanese, Thai, and Caucasian patients revealed that CD72-*1 allele correlated with nephritis in Japanese SLE patients. RT-PCR detected an alternatively spliced CD72 transcript more prevalent in *2/*2 genotypes. The interaction between FCGR2B-232Thr and CD72-*1 genotype significantly increased SLE risk (OR 4.63, 95% CI 1.47-14.6). These findings highlight the complex interplay between FCGR2B and CD72 variants in human autoimmune diseases.

title: Genetic Polymorphisms and Their Association with Prostate Cancer Risk
abstract: Recent studies have highlighted the role of genetic variations in the prostate specific antigen (PSA) gene and the androgen receptor (AR) gene in prostate cancer (PC) susceptibility. The PSA gene contains a G/A substitution in the androgen response element (ARE) region, while the AR gene exhibits polymorphic regions with variable glutamine and glycine repeats. This study investigated the association between these genetic variants and PC risk, as well as their interactions. One hundred PC patients were compared with 79 individuals with benign prostate hyperplasia (BPH) and 67 population controls. DNA was extracted from blood samples, and PSA/ARE promoter regions were amplified via PCR. Restriction enzyme analysis using Nhe 1 distinguished G/A alleles, while AR/CAG and GGC repeat lengths were quantified through fluorescence-based methods. Results showed a significantly higher frequency of PSA/GG genotypes in PC patients (30%) compared to BPH (18%) and controls (16%) (P=0.025). This effect was more pronounced in younger individuals (<65 years) with GG alleles (42%). Additionally, PC cases had a greater proportion of short CAG/GG genotypes compared to BPH and controls (P=0.006). These findings support the hypothesis that the PSA/ARE GG genotype increases PC risk, particularly in younger men, and confirm that short glutamine repeats in conjunction with GG genotypes elevate malignant disease risk. Additional indexed biomedical mentions considered for relation extraction included: glutamine repeat; CAG repeat.

title: Genetic Linkage and Molecular Analysis of Congenital Microcoria and Glaucoma in an Asian Indian Family
abstract: A rare autosomal dominant developmental disorder of the iris, congenital microcoria, is associated with myopia and juvenile open angle glaucoma. In this study, a three-generation Asian Indian family with 15 affected individuals displaying congenital microcoria (pupils < 2 mm) was analyzed for linkage to the 13q31-q32 locus. Genetic mapping identified peak two-point LOD scores of 3.5, 4.7, and 5.3 at markers D13S154, DCT, and D13S1280, with multipoint analysis confirming localization of the microcoria locus to this chromosomal region. Further, eight family members with both microcoria and glaucoma were tested for glaucoma-related genes: myocilin (MYOC), optineurin (OPTN), and CYP1B1. Direct sequencing revealed a 144 G > A mutation in exon 1 of the MYOC gene in five patients, absent in unaffected relatives and 100 controls. The study confirms the genetic homogeneity of congenital microcoria and highlights the potential link between microcoria and glaucoma, though the MYOC Q48H mutation, known to cause glaucoma in India, complicates this association. The DCT locus, part of the tyrosinase family involved in pigmentation, maps within the 6-7 cM region defining the MCOR locus. This research underscores the complex interplay between congenital microcoria, glaucoma, and the MYOC gene, with ongoing efforts to refine the MCOR locus and elucidate its role in these conditions.

title: A Novel E333D Mutation in the Thyroid Hormone Beta Receptor Linked to Resistance to Thyroid Hormone Syndrome
abstract: A novel mutation (E333D) in the thyroid hormone beta receptor causing resistance to thyroid hormone syndrome. Resistance to thyroid hormone (RTH) is a genetic disorder characterized by elevated serum thyroid hormones (TH), failure to suppress pituitary thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) secretion, and variable peripheral tissue responsiveness to TH. The disorder is associated with diverse mutations in the thyroid hormone beta receptor (TRbeta). Here, we report a novel natural RTH mutation (E333D) located in the large carboxy-terminal ligand binding domain of TRbeta. The mutation was identified in a 26-year-old Japanese man seeking medical attention due to progressive overweight. Biochemical tests revealed elevated free thyroxine (T4: 19.2 pg/ml (normal, 7.5 - 17)) and triiodothyronine (T3: 5.1 pg/ml (normal, 1.3 - 3.5)) in the serum, along with an inappropriately nonsuppressed TSH level of 4.3 mU/ml (normal, 0.3 - 4). His mother and his sister also showed biochemical abnormalities consistent with RTH. Direct sequencing of the TRbeta gene identified a heterozygous transition 1284A > C in exon 9, resulting in the substitution of glutamic acid 333 by aspartic acid residue (E333D). Further functional analyses of the novel TRbeta mutant were performed. The E333D mutation did not significantly affect the receptor's affinity for T3 or its heterodimer formation with retinoid X receptor (RXR) when bound to DNA. However, in transient transfection assays, the E333D TRbeta mutant exhibited impaired transcriptional regulation on two distinct positively regulated thyroid response elements (F2- and DR4-TREs) as well as on the negatively regulated human TSHalpha promoter. Additionally, a dominant inhibition of the wild-type TRbeta counterpart transactivation function was observed on both a positive (F2-TRE) and a negative (TSHalpha) promoter. These results strongly suggest that the E333D TRbeta mutation is responsible for the RTH phenotype in the proposita's family.

title: Germline Variants in Antioxidant Genes and Prognosis in Breast Cancer
abstract: Common germline genetic variation in antioxidant defense genes is associated with survival outcomes in breast cancer patients. This study examined the relationship between 54 polymorphisms in 10 genes involved in oxidative damage repair—CAT, SOD1, SOD2, GPX1, GPX4, GSR, TXN, TXN2, TXNRD1, and TXNRD2—and survival in 4,470 women diagnosed with breast cancer. Two single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in GPX4 (rs713041 and rs757229) were linked to all-cause mortality, even after adjusting for multiple factors. These SNPs are correlated (r² = 0.61) and are located near the selenocysteine insertion sequence in the GPX4 3' untranslated region. The rare allele of rs713041 was associated with increased mortality, with a hazard ratio of 1.27 per allele. This effect remained significant after adjusting for tumor stage, grade, and estrogen receptor status. The common allele was more highly expressed in normal lymphocytes, breast tissue, and tumors compared to the rare allele, though no differences in total GPX4 mRNA levels were observed across genotypes. These findings support the hypothesis that common genetic variation in GPX4 influences prognosis after breast cancer diagnosis. Reactive oxygen species (ROS) are implicated in DNA damage and cancer progression, highlighting the role of antioxidant pathways in disease outcomes. Additional indexed biomedical mentions considered for relation extraction included: death.

title: Genomic and Expression Profiling in Mantle Cell Lymphoma: Identifying Key Genes
abstract: Integrated genomic and expression analysis in mantle cell lymphoma (MCL) revealed critical gene-dosage regulated candidates. MCL is defined by the t(11;14)(q13;q32) translocation and additional chromosomal abnormalities, including losses of 1p, 6q, 11q, 13q, and gains of 3q, 8q. Array-comparative genomic hybridization (CGH) narrowed chromosomal imbalance intervals, but many genes within these regions remain candidates for MCL pathogenesis. Combining tiling-resolution array-CGH with gene expression data from 11 MCL samples identified genomic alterations linked to specific mRNA expression patterns. Only a subset of genes within these intervals showed consistent correlation between DNA copy number and RNA expression levels. These genes, including those involved in cyclic adenosine monophosphate-regulated pathways (PRKACB), DNA damage repair (ATM, ERCC5, FBXO5), energy metabolism, and signal transduction (ARHGAP29), are likely central to MCL development. Deregulation of these gene products may disrupt pathways critical for tumor progression and survival.

title: A Six-Nucleotide Deletion Variant in the CASP8 Promoter Region is Inversely Associated with Squamous Cell Carcinoma of the Head and Neck
abstract: The six-nucleotide deletion/insertion variant in the CASP8 promoter region is inversely associated with risk of squamous cell carcinoma of the head and neck. Caspase 8 (CASP8) is an apoptosis-related cysteine peptidase involved in the death receptor pathway and likely in the mitochondrial pathway. A CASP8 promoter region six-nucleotide deletion/insertion (-652 6N ins/del) variant and a coding region D302H polymorphism are reportedly important in cancer development, but no reported study has assessed the associations of these genetic variations with risk of head and neck cancer. In a hospital-based study of non-Hispanic whites, we genotyped CASP8 -652 6N del and 302H variants in 1,023 patients with squamous cell carcinoma of the head and neck (SCCHN) and 1,052 cancer-free controls. Crude and adjusted odds ratios (OR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) were estimated using unconditional logistic regression models. The CASP8 -652 6N del variant genotypes or haplotypes were inversely associated with SCCHN risk (adjusted OR, 0.70; 95% CI, 0.57-0.85 for the ins/del + del/del genotypes compared with the ins/ins genotype; adjusted OR, 0.73; 95% CI, 0.55-0.97 for the del-D haplotype compared with the ins-D haplotype). Furthermore, the number of the CASP8 -652 6N del (but not 302H) variant allele tended to correlate with increased levels of camptothecin-induced p53-mediated apoptosis in T lymphocytes from 170 cancer-free controls. We concluded that the CASP8 -652 6N del variant allele may contribute to the risk of developing SCCHN in non-Hispanic white populations. Further validation by population-based case-control studies and rigorous mechanistic studies is warranted.

title: NF-kB and Radiation in Tumor Immune Interactions: Role of Smac Mimetic BV6
abstract: NF-kB serves as a critical molecular bridge between tumor cells and Th1/Tc1 T cells in the tumor microenvironment, mediating radiation-induced tumor suppression.
