From 10 to 50 weeks of age, stage-specific miRNA profiling in KC mice showed downregulation of miR-216, miR-217, miR-100, miR-345, miR-141, miR-483 - 3p, miR-26b, miR-150, miR-195, Let-7b, and Let-96, and upregulation of miR-21, miR-205, miR-146b, miR-34c, miR-1273, miR-223, and miR-195 relative to controls. The miRNA expression patterns in mice correlated with those in human pancreatic cancer cell lines and tissues. Ectopic expression of Let-7b in CD18/HPAF and Capan1 cells led to reduced KRAS and MSST1 expression. This study provides insights into miRNA expression dynamics during pancreatic cancer pathogenesis, aiding in the identification of potential diagnostic/prognostic markers and therapeutic targets.

title: GADD45A and p38 Mitogen-activated protein kinase in hematopoietic stem cell differentiation
abstract: DNA-damage response gene GADD45A modulates hematopoietic stem cell (HSC) differentiation through p38 Mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) signaling. HSCs sustain blood production via self-renewal and differentiation into various lineages. GADD45A is induced by genotoxic stress in HSCs and regulates cell cycle, apoptosis, and DNA repair. While GADD45A typically arrests the cell cycle or triggers apoptosis under severe damage, its role in hematopoiesis remains debated. Here, we demonstrate that GADD45A expression drives HSC differentiation without impairing survival or cycle progression. Single-cell tracking revealed that GADD45A-expressing HSCs rapidly commit to progenitor cells within 29 hours. These cells fail to reconstitute blood in vivo due to multilineage differentiation. Notably, g-irradiation induces GADD45A expression, which activates p38 MAPK signaling and promotes megakaryocytic-erythroid, myeloid, and lymphoid lineage development. These findings suggest that genotoxic stress-induced GADD45A directs HSCs toward differentiation, preventing fatal transformation.

title: Cisplatin Induces Tolerogenic Dendritic Cells via IL-10 in TLR-Activated Inflammatory Conditions
abstract: Cisplatin induces tolerogenic dendritic cells in response to TLR agonists through the abundant production of IL-10, promoting Th2- and Tr1-biased T-cell immunity. While cisplatin's role in cancer therapy is well-established, its immunomodulatory effects on dendritic cells (DCs) remain poorly understood. Here, we investigate how cisplatin modulates DC functionality and signaling pathways upon TLR stimulation. Cisplatin-treated DCs down-regulate cell surface molecules including CD80, CD86, and MHC class I and II, while up-regulating endocytic capacity in a dose-dependent manner. TLR agonist stimulation of cisplatin-treated DCs significantly increases IL-10 production via p38 MAPK and NF-kappaB pathways without altering TNF-alpha or IL-12p70 levels, indicating tolerogenic DC induction. This effect relies on IL-10 production, as DCs from IL-10-/- mice or IL-10-neutralized DCs fail to generate tolerogenic cells. Interestingly, co-treatment with cisplatin and lipopolysaccharide (LPS) reduces immunostimulatory capacity for Th1- and Th17-type T cells, shifting toward Th2-type immunity. In vitro and in vivo studies reveal an increased population of IL-10-producing CD3+CD4+LAG-3+CD49b+CD25-Foxp3- Tr1 cells without affecting Foxp3+ regulatory T cells. These findings suggest that cisplatin induces immune-suppressive tolerogenic DCs in TLR agonist-induced inflammatory conditions through abundant IL-10 production, skewing Th cell differentiation toward Th2 and Tr1 subsets. This mechanism may provide cancer cells with an opportunity to evade immune surveillance.

title: Role of Angiotensin II Receptor Signaling in Liver Metastasis of Colorectal Cancer
abstract: The renin-angiotensin system plays a critical role in tumor progression and metastatic spread. In this study, the impact of Angiotensin II subtype 1a receptor signaling on liver metastasis formation was investigated. Mice with genetic deletion of AT1a receptor (AT1aKO) exhibited reduced liver weight and lower metastatic rates compared to wild-type (C57BL/6) mice. mRNA levels of CD31, transforming growth factor- b1, and F4/80 were significantly downregulated in AT1aKO mice. Immunofluorescence analysis revealed higher accumulation of TGF-b1-positive F4/80-positive cells in metastatic regions of WT mice. Bone marrow transfer experiments showed that AT1aKO-BM cells formed fewer metastases than WT-BM cells, but WT-BM cells transferred to AT1aKO hosts produced even fewer metastases. These findings suggest that resident hepatic macrophages drive metastasis through TGF-b1 signaling. Treatment with clodronate liposomes suppressed metastasis by reducing TGF-b1-positive F4/80-positive cell accumulation. Collagen deposition in metastatic areas was closely associated with AT1a signaling. These results indicate that the renin-angiotensin system promotes liver metastasis via TGF-b1-mediated mechanisms. Additional indexed biomedical mentions considered for relation extraction included: colorectal cancer.

title: Genetic Variants and Metabolic Risk Factors in Diabetes Development
abstract: Polymorphisms in the SLC2A2 gene are associated with the conversion from impaired glucose tolerance to type 2 diabetes. The study examined the role of SLC2A2, GCK, GLP1R, TCF1, HNF4A, GIP, and insulin in predicting the transition from impaired glucose tolerance (IGT) to type 2 diabetes. rs5393, a variant in SLC2A2, was found to increase the risk of type 2 diabetes by threefold in the entire study population. Obese individuals with IGT showed a higher risk for type 2 diabetes in the control group, but not in the intervention group. Impaired glucose tolerance is linked to the expression of TCF1 and GLP1R, while insulin and GCK are involved in glucose regulation. The association between rs5393 and type 2 diabetes remains significant in the context of obesity and impaired glucose tolerance.

title: A Canadian Family with Familial Partial Lipodystrophy Type 3 and PPARG Mutation Y355X
abstract: A Canadian family with familial partial lipodystrophy type 3 (FPLD3) was studied, characterized by heterozygous mutations in PPARG encoding peroxisomal proliferator-activated receptor-gamma. The affected mother exhibited loss of fat on arms and legs, along with profound insulin resistance, diabetes, severe hypertriglyceridemia, and relapsing pancreatitis. Her pre-pubescent daughter had normal fat distribution but elevated plasma triglycerides, C-peptide, and depressed high-density lipoprotein cholesterol. Both were heterozygous for PPARG nonsense mutation Y355X, whose protein product was transcriptionally inactive and markedly unstable. These findings suggest that PPAR-gamma deficiency, whether through haploinsufficiency or dominant-negative interference, contributes to the FPLD3 phenotype. Additional indexed biomedical mentions considered for relation extraction included: Peroxisomal proliferator activated receptor-gamma.

title: Catechol-O-Methyltransferase and Val158Met Polymorphisms in Opiate Addiction
abstract: Catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT) gene variants, particularly the Val158Met polymorphism, may be associated with opiate addiction in Hispanic populations. COMT catalyzes the metabolism of catechol neurotransmitters, such as dopamine, which is involved in drug reward mechanisms. A common single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP), G472A, results in a Val158Met substitution, causing a fourfold decrease in COMT activity. We sequenced exon IV of the COMT gene to identify novel polymorphisms and genotyped four of the five detected variants using TaqMan assay on 266 opioid-dependent individuals and 173 control subjects. Genotype distributions of the G472A SNP showed significant variation (P = 0.029) across Caucasians, Hispanics, and African Americans. Analysis revealed a trend toward association (P = 0.053) between the G472A SNP in Hispanic subjects and opiate addiction, with significant findings in women but not in men. Dopamine levels were found to have a negative correlation with COMT activity, suggesting a regulatory relationship. Catechol neurotransmitters exhibited a negative correlation with COMT activity, indicating a potential inhibitory effect. No significant associations were found with haplotypes of the three most common SNPs, and linkage disequilibrium patterns were consistent across ethnic groups.

title: POLG1 Mutations and Associated Clinical Phenotypes in Patients with Movement Disorder and Hepatoencephalopathy
abstract: Depletion of mitochondrial DNA in fibroblast cultures from patients with POLG1 mutations is linked to catalytic domain defects. This study examined clinical and cellular features of 24 children with POLG1 mutations, focusing on the alpha subunit of the mitochondrial DNA gamma polymerase. Twenty-one patients exhibited Alpers syndrome, the most severe autosomal recessive phenotype, characterized by hepatoencephalopathy and mtDNA depletion. Cellular mtDNA levels correlated more closely with genotype than clinical manifestations. Patients with tissue mtDNA depletion showed mutations in either a catalytic domain or a nonsense mutation. Four out of 12 patients displayed a progressive, mosaic pattern of mtDNA depletion, all with mutations in both POLG1 alleles. Those with two linker mutations had normal mtDNA levels and milder phenotypes. Epilepsy and/or movement disorder were prominent features in all 21 patients. Previous research suggested replication stalling as a mechanism for mtDNA depletion, with the mosaic pattern indicating severe stalling. One patient with a severe phenotype was a compound heterozygote with mutations in both polymerase and exonuclease domains. This highlights the necessity of both polymerase and 3'-5' exonuclease activities in POLG1 function, consistent with functional models of DNA polymerases.

title: Genetic Mutations and Kidney Disease Phenotypes
abstract: Mutations in phospholipase C epsilon 1 are associated with diffuse mesangial sclerosis, which may occur as an isolated finding or in conjunction with congenital or infantile nephrotic syndrome. A four-basepair deletion in the PLCE1 gene was identified in three individuals of Pakistani descent with diffuse mesangial sclerosis who also exhibited congenital or infantile nephrotic syndrome. Genome-wide analysis revealed that all affected individuals were homozygous for this deletion, which leads to a premature stop codon. The asymptomatic father of two patients was found to carry the same mutation, suggesting possible nonpenetrance. While the deletion is linked to diffuse mesangial sclerosis, no direct association was found between the mutation and congenital or infantile nephrotic syndrome. Additionally, no relation was observed between phospholipase C epsilon 1 and the four-basepair deletion, except for their shared role in kidney disease pathology.

title: Levofloxacin-Induced Seizures and CYP1A2 Inhibition: A Case Report and Literature Review
abstract: This report describes a patient who developed seizures following initiation of levofloxacin therapy. The case is discussed in the context of potential drug interactions involving the inhibition of cytochrome P450 ( CYP ) 1A2 by levofloxacin. Literature review identifies six documented cases of levofloxacin-induced seizures, with evidence suggesting that CYP1A2 inhibition may contribute to the clinical manifestations. The study highlights the importance of monitoring patients on levofloxacin who are also receiving medications metabolized by CYP1A2.

title: Carbamazepine-Induced Myocarditis and Hypersensitivity Phenotypes
abstract: Carbamazepine has been associated with severe hypersensitivity reactions, including eosinophilic myocarditis and cardiogenic shock. A rare but fatal complication of carbamazepine therapy is hypersensitivity myocarditis, which is characterized by myocardial infiltration and myocyte damage. This case report highlights the association between carbamazepine and hypersensitivity, as well as the severe outcomes of drug hypersensitivity, such as death and myocarditis. The cardiovascular system is particularly vulnerable to carbamazepine-induced adverse effects, with cardiogenic shock being a common cause of mortality. Hypersensitivity reactions to carbamazepine may manifest as myocarditis, a condition that can lead to fatal outcomes. The clinical presentation of this condition often lacks early warning signs, leading to diagnosis post-mortem. Histological findings in this case revealed extensive eosinophilic infiltration, confirming the presence of myocarditis and hypersensitivity.

title: No Association Between ADRA2B-4825 Gene Insertion/Deletion and Migraine in a Japanese Population
abstract: This study investigated the association between the ADRA2B-4825 gene insertion/deletion polymorphism and migraine in a sample of Japanese individuals. A case-control design was employed, including 420 migraine cases and 630 control subjects. Genomic DNA was extracted from peripheral blood samples, and PCR was used to amplify the region containing the -4825 insertion/deletion site. Data were adjusted for age, sex, and family history of migraine. Logistic regression analysis revealed no significant correlation between the ADRA2B-4825 gene insertion/deletion and migraine status, either at the allele or genotype level. The 12-nucleotide insertion/deletion in the ADRA2B promoter region was also evaluated, but no association was observed with migraine occurrence. These findings suggest that the ADRA2B-4825 polymorphism may not play a role in migraine susceptibility in this population. Additional indexed biomedical mentions considered for relation extraction included: 12-nucleotide insertion/deletion ( indel ).

title: Novel Compound Heterozygous Mutation in MLYCD Gene in a Patient with Malonic Aciduria and Associated Phenotypes
abstract: A 4-year-old Japanese boy presented with malonic aciduria, characterized by developmental delay, short stature, and brain abnormalities. Laboratory analysis revealed elevated levels of malonic acid and methylmalonic acid in urine. Genetic testing of the MLYCD gene identified a compound heterozygous mutation, including c.920T > G (p. Leu307Arg) and a deletion in exon 1. The missense mutation (c.920T > G) was not detected in 100 unrelated healthy controls. This case expands the known spectrum of MLYCD mutations associated with malonic aciduria, highlighting the genetic basis of the disease and its clinical features.

title: Genetic Variants in Uroplakin Genes and Their Association with Vesicoureteral Reflux and Nephropathy
abstract: The role of human uroplakin genes in primary vesicoureteral reflux (VUR) remains poorly understood, highlighting potential contributions to disease heterogeneity. BACKGROUND: VUR is a hereditary disorder characterized by retrograde urine flow into the ureters and kidneys, affecting approximately 1% of young children. It is a significant cause of end-stage renal failure in both children and adults. Recent studies in mice suggest that genetic ablation of uroplakin (UP) III gene, which encodes a 47 kD urothelial-specific integral membrane protein forming urothelial plaques, leads to VUR and hydronephrosis. METHODS: To investigate potential mutations in UP genes associated with human VUR, we analyzed all four UP genes in 76 patients with radiologically confirmed VUR through PCR amplification and sequencing of exons and flanking intronic sequences. RESULTS: Eighteen single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) were identified, with seven being missense mutations and no truncation or frame shift mutations. Healthy controls, including 90 race-matched individuals unrelated to the VUR patients, were used for association analysis. Most SNPs showed no significant association with VUR. However, SNP1 of UP Ia gene affecting a C to T conversion and an Ala7Val change, and SNP7 of UP III affecting a C to G conversion and a Pro154Ala change, were marginally associated with VUR (both P=0.08). Additional case studies confirmed a weak association of UP III SNP7 in VUR (P=0.036 adjusted for subsets). CONCLUSION: The weak association and lack of simple Mendelian inheritance suggest that missense changes in uroplakin genes may contribute to a complex polygenic disease rather than a dominant cause of VUR. The absence of truncation mutations in patients, combined with findings in UP III knockout mice showing VUR, hydronephrosis, and neonatal death, indicates that major uroplakin mutations could be embryonically or postnatally lethal in humans. Additional indexed biomedical mentions considered for relation extraction included: nephropathy; uroplakin ( UP ) III.

title: Potential Association of Domperidone and Mirtazapine with Restless Legs Syndrome
abstract: Does domperidone exacerbate mirtazapine-associated restless legs syndrome? Recent evidence highlights the dopaminergic system's role in restless legs syndrome (RLS). For instance, levodopa and dopamine agonists significantly alleviate RLS symptoms, while dopamine D2 receptor antagonists can induce or worsen RLS. There is no prior report on whether domperidone, a peripheral dopamine D2 receptor antagonist, might similarly trigger RLS. Mirtazapine, a noradrenergic and specific serotonergic antidepressant (NaSSA), has been linked to RLS in multiple studies. A case report describes a depressed patient with postprandial dyspepsia who developed RLS after initiating mirtazapine alongside domperidone. RLS symptoms resolved upon discontinuation of mirtazapine, suggesting no potentiating effect of domperidone on mirtazapine-associated RLS. However, clinicians should remain vigilant about mirtazapine's potential to cause RLS, particularly in patients using concomitant dopamine D2 receptor antagonists. The dopamine D2 receptor's involvement in RLS is further underscored by the negative correlation between levodopa and RLS symptoms, as well as the drug interaction between domperidone and mirtazapine in this case.

title: Mutational Analysis of VWF in Type 2A VWD Patients
abstract: L1503R is a mutation in the VWF gene associated with type 2A von Willebrand disease. Type 2A von Willebrand disease (VWD) is characterized by impaired function of von Willebrand factor (VWF), which is linked to reduced high-molecular-weight multimers. Sequence analysis of the VWF gene from two unrelated patients with type 2A VWD revealed an identical heterozygous T→G transversion at nucleotide 4508, resulting in the L1503R substitution in the VWF A2 domain. This mutation was not present in 60 normal individuals and was expressed in 293 T cells, where only trace amounts of the mutant VWF were secreted, while most remained intracellular. Co-transfection experiments with wild-type and mutant plasmids showed a dominant-negative effect, with increased mutant DNA leading to reduced VWF secretion. Molecular dynamics simulations indicated structural changes in L1503R, affecting VWF stability. ADAMTS13, a protease involved in VWF processing, is not directly associated with this mutation, though it may influence VWF degradation. VWF and ADAMTS13 are gene products with no direct functional link in this context.

title: Genetic and Historical Factors in the Distribution of the CCR5-Delta32 Allele
abstract: The geographic distribution of the CCR5-Delta32 allele, a variant of the chemokine receptor gene, has been linked to historical events in Europe. This study examines the influence of ancient Mediterranean civilizations' expansion on the prevalence of this mutation. The CCR5-Delta32 allele is primarily found in Europe and Western Asia, showing a north-south gradient in frequency. Homozygous individuals carrying this mutation exhibit resistance to HIV-1 infection and delayed progression to AIDS. However, the mutation's origin is not directly tied to HIV, as the virus emerged too recently to influence its spread. The allele frequency in Europe correlates with historical factors, including the timing of early colonization and proximity to the Roman Empire's northern borders. Additionally, the CCR5-Delta32 mutation has been identified in ancient DNA samples dating back over 7000 years, indicating a long-standing presence in European populations. In the context of West Nile virus, the chemokine receptor plays a role in antimicrobial defense, highlighting the gene's pathogen-specific functions. These findings suggest that the current distribution of the CCR5-Delta32 allele may be due to historical factors rather than recent genetic spread, with the mutation's persistence possibly linked to resistance against imported infections.

title: Dioxin-like Compounds and AHR Polymorphism Analysis in Human Populations
abstract: The study investigates the relationship between dioxin-like chemicals and the aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AHR) in human populations. 2,3,7,8-tetrachlorodibenzo-p-dioxin binds to the AHR, activating it through a mechanism that varies among individuals due to genetic polymorphisms. Analysis of AHR gene sequences from six ethnic groups revealed limited polymorphisms in the ligand binding region, with only six exonic SNPs identified. Four of these SNPs resulted in amino acid changes, while two were synonymous. The dioxin-like chemical's interaction with the AHR highlights the importance of genetic variability in determining individual susceptibility to dioxin effects.

title: SLURP1 Mutation and T-Cell Dysfunction in Mal de Meleda Patients
abstract: SLURP1 mutations have been linked to impaired T-cell activation in individuals with mal de Meleda. Mal de Meleda (MDM) is a rare autosomal recessive disorder characterized by palmoplantar erythrokeratoderma, caused by mutations in the SLURP1 gene. SLURP1 functions as an allosteric agonist for the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (nAchR), which is crucial for maintaining epidermal homeostasis. In addition, nAchR signaling plays a key role in regulating T-cell activity. Among patients with MDM, those carrying the G to A substitution in nucleotide 256 of the SLURP1 gene (resulting in a glycine to arginine substitution at amino acid 86, G86R) are at increased risk for melanoma and viral infection. These conditions may be associated with defective T-cell function and disrupted epidermal homeostasis. A study of a Taiwanese family with MDM revealed that individuals with the heterozygous or homozygous G86R mutation exhibited reduced T-cell activation. Treatment with recombinant human SLURP-1 protein restored normal T-cell function. These findings suggest that the presence of the G86R mutation in SLURP1 may contribute to T-cell dysfunction in MDM patients, highlighting the importance of SLURP1 in maintaining immune cell function. Additional indexed biomedical mentions considered for relation extraction included: anti-CD3/anti-CD28.

title: Genetic Variants in IRS2 and Their Association with Obesity and Diabetes-Related Traits in a Hispanic Population
abstract: A study was conducted to investigate genetic variations in the IRS2 gene and their potential links to obesity and diabetes-related characteristics in Hispanic individuals. Exonic and intronic regions, along with 5' and 3' flanking sequences of IRS2 (14.5 kb), were sequenced in 934 Hispanic participants to identify single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs). Additionally, 15 SNPs from Illumina HumanOmni1-Quad BeadChips were analyzed. Genotype data were examined for associations between SNPs and obesity, as well as diabetes-related traits. Bayesian analysis was employed to determine the most probable functional SNPs. A total of 140 SNPs were identified, with minor allele frequencies ranging from 0.001 to 0.47. Forty-two of the 70 coding SNPs resulted in amino acid substitutions. SNP 10510452_139 in the promoter region showed a strong association with obesity-related traits, contributing 2-4% to body weight variation. However, none of the SNPs or indels were linked to diabetes-related traits or fasting glucose homeostasis. These findings suggest that rare IRS2 variants may influence body weight regulation but not fasting glucose control in this population.

title: Zolmitriptan and Takotsubo Syndrome: A Case Report
abstract: Zolmitriptan has been implicated in cases of Takotsubo syndrome (TS), a condition characterized by left ventricular apical ballooning and electrocardiographic changes suggestive of acute coronary syndrome. A 56-year-old woman with a history of mitral valve prolapse and migraines was admitted for substernal chest pain. Her electrocardiogram revealed 1.5 mm ST-segment elevation in leads II, III, aVF, V5, and V6, with elevated troponin I levels. Coronary angiography showed normal coronary arteries but moderate left ventricular ejection fraction with wall motion abnormalities consistent with TS. Retrospective history indicated she used zolmitriptan sparingly for migraines but had previously taken it 2-3 times daily for several days. She reported no recent stress or migrainous episodes. Literature suggests zolmitriptan may induce coronary artery vasospasm, though no prior cases linked to TS were documented. Her condition resolved without further complications, highlighting the need for careful monitoring of zolmitriptan use in patients with cardiovascular risk factors.

title: T Follicular Helper Cell Subpopulations and Their Role in B-Cell Maturation
abstract: CD25(+) Bcl6(low ) T follicular helper cells play a critical role in supporting maturation of B cells within germinal centers of human tonsil. The majority of CXCR5(+) PD1(+) CD4(+) T follicular helper (Tfh) cells (>90%) are CD25(-) Bcl6(high ), while a small subpopulation (<10%) are CD25(+) Bcl6(low ) but do not express FoxP3 and are not regulatory cells. Purified T:B-cell conjugates from tonsils were enriched for CD25(+) Bcl6(low ) Tfh cells. In response to IL-2, these CD25(+) Tfh cells upregulate costimulatory molecules ICOS and OX40, increase transcription factor cMaf expression, produce cytokines IL-21, IL-17, and IL-10, and enhance antiapoptotic protein Bcl2 levels. Conjugates formed with CD25(+) Bcl6(low ) Tfh cells include B cells expressing higher levels of activation-induced cytidine deaminase (AID), memory marker CD45RO, surface IgG or IgA, and MHC class II compared to conjugates with CD25(-) Bcl6(high ) Tfh cells. While IL-2 inhibits early Tfh-cell differentiation, Tfh-cell recognition of antigen-presenting B cells and signaling through the T-cell receptor likely triggers expression of the high-affinity IL-2 receptor and responses to IL-2 including downregulation of Bcl6. CD25 expression on Tfh cells and local IL-2 production in tonsil or lymph node may sustain B helper T-cell function during later stages of B-cell maturation and immune memory development.

title: Splicing Variants of Filamin B in Giant Cell Tumor of Bone
abstract: Differential expression of filamin B splice variants is observed in giant cell tumor cells. Giant cell tumor of bone (GCT) is the most commonly reported non-malignant bone tumor in Hong Kong. This type of tumor typically affects individuals aged 20-40 years and is known for local recurrence, especially when incomplete removal occurs. Filamins are actin-binding proteins with three family members: filamin A, B, and C. They are encoded by three distinct genes, FLNA, FLNB, and FLNC, which produce various transcript variants across different cell types. In this study, the effects of FLNBv2 and FLNBv4 on GCT cells were investigated. The primary distinction between FLNBv2 and FLNBv4 is the absence of the hinge 1 region in FLNBv4. Analysis revealed that the relative abundance of FLNBv4 varies among different GCT cell lines, while its expression in normal osteoblasts is only minimally detectable. Functionally, overexpression of FLNBv4 leads to increased levels of RANKL, OCN, OPG, and RUNX2, which are closely linked to GCT cell survival and differentiation. Additionally, FLNBv4 has a negative impact on the viability of GCT cells compared to FLNBv2. In conclusion, splicing variants of FLNB exhibit differential expression in GCT cells and may contribute to the proliferation and differentiation of tumor cells.

title: Spirulina Lipopolysaccharides Modulate Cytokine Balance to Inhibit Tumor Progression
abstract: Spirulina lipopolysaccharides inhibit tumor growth in a Toll-like receptor 4-dependent manner by altering the cytokine milieu from interleukin-17/interleukin-23 to interferon-g. Th17 cells and their cytokine interleukin (IL)-17 play a critical role in tumor progression. IL-6 and IL-23 are essential for Th17 differentiation and propagation. Bacterial lipopolysaccharides stimulate immune cells to produce these inflammatory cytokines. Spirulina LPS exhibits low toxicity and does not induce IL-6 or IL-23 in mice. In a hepatoma model, Spirulina LPS suppressed tumor growth in C3H/HeN mice but not in TLR4-mutant mice, reducing IL-17 and IL-23 levels while increasing interferon-g. The antitumor effects are mediated by T cells. In vitro, Spirulina LPS impairs antigen-presenting function, limiting IL-17-producing cell generation via TLR4. Anti-IL-17 antibody administration in tumor-bearing mice significantly reduced tumor growth and enhanced interferon-g responses. These findings support the role of IFN-g and IL-17/IL-23 in regulating Th17 and Th1 responses. Spirulina LPS modulates the IFN-g-IL-17/IL-23 axis toward IFN-g production, inhibiting tumor growth. Additionally, Spirulina LPS suppresses spontaneous mammary tumor development, highlighting its potential as a TLR-based immunomodulator for cancer therapy. Additional indexed biomedical mentions considered for relation extraction included: mammary tumors.

title: Role of Insulin-like Growth Factor 1 Receptor-Mediated Pathways in Hypoxia-Induced Cell Survival
abstract: Hypoxia significantly influences cell survival through the activation of the Insulin-like growth factor 1 receptor-mediated signaling pathway, which modulates the PI3K/Akt/mTOR axis. Reactive oxygen species (ROS) are closely linked to hypoxia, with increased ROS production observed under hypoxic conditions. The chemical inhibitor 3-methyladenine suppresses autophagy, which in turn affects ROS levels and apoptosis. LY294002, a PI3K inhibitor, disrupts the PI3K/Akt/mTOR pathway, leading to reduced autophagy and enhanced ROS generation. Insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1) plays a critical role in maintaining cell viability under hypoxia by promoting autophagy and scavenging ROS. The Insulin-like growth factor 1 receptor-mediated pathway is associated with the PI3K/Akt/mTOR signaling cascade, which is inhibited by LY294002. These findings highlight the complex interplay between hypoxia, ROS, and the PI3K/Akt/mTOR pathway in regulating cell survival.

title: Estrogen Modulates Receptor-Mediated Hypotension in Female Rats
abstract: This study examines the interaction between estrogen and alpha2-adrenergic and I1-imidazoline receptor-mediated hypotension in female rats. We found that estrogen negatively modulates the hypotensive effects of clonidine, a mixed alpha2-/I1-receptor agonist, in estrogen-replaced rats. The present investigation assessed the impact of estrogen on alpha2- and I1-receptor activation by comparing the responses of sham-operated, ovariectomized (Ovx), and estrogen-replaced rats to intraperitoneal injections of rilmenidine (600 μg/kg) and alpha-methyldopa (100 mg/kg). These agents selectively activate I1- and alpha2-receptors, respectively. Blood pressure, hemodynamic variability, and locomotor activity were monitored in radiotelemetered animals. In sham-operated rats, both drugs induced similar hypotension lasting over 5 hours, accompanied by decreased mean arterial pressure variability. SDRR was only reduced by alpha-methyldopa. Ovx rats exhibited enhanced alpha-methyldopa-induced hypotension, with further reduced SDRR and decreased locomotor activity. Estrogen replacement restored these effects to sham-operated levels. These findings indicate that estrogen downregulates alpha2- but not I1-receptor-mediated hypotension, highlighting the role of cardiac autonomic control in estrogen-alpha-methyldopa interactions. Additional indexed biomedical mentions considered for relation extraction included: a reduced locomotor activity; 17beta-estradiol.

title: Effects of the Antidepressant Trazodone on Dopamine-Dependent Behaviors in Mice
abstract: The impact of trazodone, a 5-HT 2A/2C receptor antagonist, on dopamine-dependent behaviors was investigated in mice. 5-Hydroxytryptamine, through activation of 5-HT 2C receptors, exerts a tonic inhibitory effect on dopaminergic neurotransmission, while 5-HT 2A receptor activation enhances dopamine release. Trazodone, as a 5-HT 2A/2C receptor antagonist, was evaluated for its effects on behaviors linked to the nigrostriatal DAergic system. Pretreatment with trazodone influenced dexamphetamine- and apomorphine-induced oral stereotypies, haloperidol- and apomorphine-induced catalepsy, ergometrine-induced wet dog shake behavior, and fluoxetine-induced penile erections. Trazodone at 2.5-20 mg/kg did not induce catalepsy but enhanced dexamphetamine stereotypy and antagonized haloperidol catalepsy, ergometrine-induced WDS behavior, and fluoxetine-induced erections. At higher doses (30-50 mg/kg), trazodone induced catalepsy and antagonized apomorphine and dexamphetamine stereotypies. These findings suggest that trazodone blocks 5-HT 2C receptors at lower doses, releasing nigrostriatal DAergic neurons from tonic inhibition, thereby enhancing dexamphetamine stereotypy and antagonizing haloperidol catalepsy. However, at higher doses, it blocks postsynaptic D2 DA receptors, leading to catalepsy and altered stereotypic responses.

title: Antipsychotic Agents and Metabolic Effects in Schizophrenia
abstract: This study examines the metabolic effects of antipsychotic agents in patients with schizophrenia and schizoaffective disorder. Glucose metabolism was assessed in individuals treated with clozapine, olanzapine, and risperidone. Insulin resistance was observed in patients receiving clozapine and olanzapine compared to those on risperidone. The association between glucose and insulin levels was analyzed, revealing significant differences in fasting serum insulin concentrations among the groups. Additionally, the relationship between antipsychotic agents and diabetes mellitus was explored, highlighting the potential impact of these medications on metabolic health. The study also evaluated the correlation between antipsychotic agents and insulin resistance, demonstrating that clozapine and olanzapine are linked to increased insulin resistance. Furthermore, the effects of antipsychotic agents on glucose effectiveness were investigated, showing that clozapine and olanzapine are associated with reduced glucose effectiveness compared to risperidone. These findings underscore the importance of monitoring metabolic parameters in patients treated with these medications.

title: Temporal Dynamics of Oxidative Stress Markers, Liver Toxicity, and Metabolite Levels in Rats Treated with Valproic Acid
abstract: A single dose of Valproic acid (VPA), an antiepileptic drug, was administered to adult male Sprague-Dawley rats for 3, 5, 8, 11, or 14 days. VPA was associated with oxidative stress, as indicated by elevated levels of 15-F(2t)-isoprostane. Plasma and liver lipid hydroperoxides were not elevated until day 8, while thiobarbituric acid reactive substances increased by day 14. Liver toxicity was assessed by serum alpha-glutathione S-transferase levels and histological analysis. Serum alpha-glutathione S-transferase levels rose significantly by day 5, correlating with inflammation of the liver capsule, necrosis, and steatosis. The levels of 4-ene-VPA and (E)-2,4-diene-VPA remained stable throughout the study. These findings suggest that VPA induces oxidative stress, which precedes the development of necrosis, steatosis, and elevated alpha-glutathione S-transferase levels. Additionally, Valproic acid treatment was linked to increased steatosis, highlighting its potential role in liver toxicity.

title: Dexrazoxane's Role in Mitigating Hematologic and Cardiac Toxicities from Anthracyclines and Etoposide
abstract: Dexrazoxane is effective in reducing myelosuppression caused by etoposide and daunorubicin but not doxorubicin. The anthracyclines daunorubicin, doxorubicin, and the epipodophyllotoxin etoposide are commonly used in cancer therapy, though their hematologic toxicity and cardiac effects limit clinical use. Dexrazoxane, known for its cardioprotective properties against anthracyclines, was tested for its impact on the toxicity of these drugs. In experiments, human and murine blood progenitor cells were evaluated for sensitivity to etoposide, daunorubicin, and doxorubicin with or without Dexrazoxane in colony-forming assays. In vivo, B6D2F1 mice received these drugs at varying doses with or without Dexrazoxane, and hematologic parameters were analyzed. Results showed that non-toxic doses of Dexrazoxane decreased myelosuppression and weight loss from daunorubicin and etoposide, counteracting their antiproliferative effects in assays. However, Dexrazoxane did not alleviate myelosuppression, weight loss, or cytotoxicity from doxorubicin. These findings suggest that Dexrazoxane may not reduce hematologic activity or antitumor efficacy from doxorubicin, but its strong effect on daunorubicin could affect treatment outcomes. The data also indicate that etoposide doses might be increased with Dexrazoxane use. Clinical trials are ongoing to combine Dexrazoxane with high-dose etoposide in patients with metastases to enhance efficacy while minimizing hematologic toxicity. If successful, this approach offers a mechanism to pharmacologically manage side effects from chemotherapy. Additional indexed biomedical mentions considered for relation extraction included: cardiac toxicity.

title: Ritanserin Modulates Scopolamine-Induced Amnesia via 5-HT2 Receptor Interaction
abstract: Intracerebroventricular administration of ritanserin enhanced scopolamine-induced amnesia in aged female rats. The role of ritanserin (5-HT2 antagonist) in modulating scopolamine (muscarinic cholinergic antagonist)-induced memory deficits was evaluated using the Y-maze test. Rats were grouped into six cohorts and received bilateral cannulae in the hippocampal CA1 region. Two weeks later, they were administered saline, DMSO, scopolamine (2 µg/0.5 µl saline), ritanserin (2, 4, and 8 µg/0.5 µl DMSO), and combined treatments (scopolamine + ritanserin) via cannulae daily. Behavioral assessments were conducted over five consecutive days, with the hidden platform's position altered on the fifth day to assess spatial and non-spatial memory. Scopolamine-treated animals exhibited prolonged exploration times and increased locomotor activity compared to saline controls. Rats receiving ritanserin (4 µg/0.5 µl/side) showed reduced exploration times and movement distances, whereas combined treatment significantly reversed the scopolamine-induced deficits. These results suggest that ritanserin's effect on scopolamine-induced amnesia is mediated through 5-HT2 receptor modulation.

title: Effects of Ecstasy Use on Serotonin-Related Neurological Outcomes
abstract: This study examines the relationship between ecstasy use and neurological outcomes, including memory impairment and neurotoxic lesions. Ecstasy was found to correlate positively with memory impairment and neurotoxic lesions, both of which are linked to serotonin levels. The serotonin transporter gene showed no significant association with memory impairment or neurotoxic lesions. However, ecstasy and serotonin demonstrated a positive correlation, with heavy use associated with long-term memory deficits. No effect of the serotonin transporter polymorphism or gender was observed in the study, highlighting the distinct roles of these factors in cognitive and neurological changes.

title: Protective Effects of Mangiferin on Biochemical Alterations and Antioxidant Status in Isoproterenol-Induced Myocardial Infarction in Rats
abstract: The study investigated the role of mangiferin, a polyphenol derived from Mangifera indica Linn., in mitigating biochemical changes and antioxidant status in isoproterenol-induced myocardial infarction (MI) in rats. Subcutaneous administration of isoproterenol (200 mg/kg body weight) for two consecutive days resulted in myocardial damage, evidenced by elevated serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) and creatine phosphokinase isoenzymes (CK-MB) levels, increased uric acid concentration, and reduced plasma iron binding capacity. The protective effects of mangiferin were assessed using triphenyl tetrazolium chloride (TTC) testing to evaluate ischemic myocardium. Heart tissue antioxidant enzymes, including superoxide dismutase, catalase, glutathione peroxidase, glutathione transferase, and glutathione reductase, were altered in MI rats. Non-enzymatic antioxidants such as cerruloplasmin, Vitamin C, Vitamin E, and glutathione levels were also affected. Pretreatment with mangiferin (100 mg/kg body weight) for 28 days significantly restored these parameters to normal levels. Administration of mangiferin elevated enzymatic antioxidant activities and serum non-enzymatic antioxidant concentrations compared to MI rats. The findings indicate that mangiferin exerts protective effects against isoproterenol-induced MI through its antioxidant properties, regulating the body's defense mechanisms against cardiac damage. Additional indexed biomedical mentions considered for relation extraction included: dimethyl sulphoxide.

title: Cardiovascular Effects of Cyclooxygenase Inhibitors: Variability in Risk Profiles
abstract: Cyclooxygenase inhibitors are associated with increased cardiovascular risk, including myocardial infarction, stroke, hypertension, and heart failure. Studies indicate that these agents may contribute to complex changes in prostanoid profiles, affecting renal, vascular, and cardiac function. The incidence of adverse cardiovascular events correlates with higher daily doses and prolonged exposure. While diagnostic markers like N-terminal pro brain natriuretic peptide and C-reactive protein show promise in identifying at-risk patients, their utility depends on individual clinical contexts. Comparative analyses of selective and unselective inhibitors highlight substance-specific differences, potentially influenced by pharmacokinetic factors. Cardiovascular adverse events, such as myocardial infarction and stroke, are more prevalent in patients with concurrent risk factors. Prostanoid modulation may also impact fluid retention and vascular resistance, underscoring the need for careful monitoring in clinical settings.

title: Alcohol and Amphetamine Effects on Fetal Growth and Drug Abuse Outcomes
abstract: Alcohol exposure during pregnancy is associated with fetal growth impairment, as demonstrated in this study. The impact of alcohol consumption on fetal development was compared to that of Amphetamine abuse, which was linked to larger cranial to body growth ratios. Drug abuse was not found to have a direct relationship with either alcohol or Amphetamine use in this cohort. The findings support early abstinence from alcohol to prevent fetal growth issues, while Amphetamine abuse was identified as a separate factor influencing cranial growth.

title: Modulation of Norepinephrine Transporter by Desipramine and Its Impact on Local Anesthetic-Induced Convulsions
abstract: Long-term use of desipramine, a norepinephrine transporter inhibitor, was associated with altered sensitivity to local-anesthetics-induced convulsions in mice. Studies revealed that repeated dosing of desipramine decreased [(3)H]norepinephrine uptake in hippocampal P2 fractions but not in other brain regions. Co-administration of lidocaine, bupivacaine, or tricaine counteracted this effect. Chronic cocaine administration increased [(3)H]norepinephrine uptake in the hippocampus, while desipramine treatment elevated lidocaine-induced convulsions and reduced cocaine-induced convulsions. Combining lidocaine with desipramine reversed the modified convulsive activity caused by repeated desipramine use. These findings suggest that desipramine-induced down-regulation of hippocampal norepinephrine transporter function may contribute to sensitization of lidocaine convulsions. Inhibition of Na(+ ) channels by local anesthetics could regulate this desipramine-mediated down-regulation of transporter function. Repeated cocaine exposure up-regulated hippocampal norepinephrine transporter activity, indicating distinct mechanisms for desipramine-induced convulsions compared to cocaine-kindling effects.

title: Pharmacological Potential of Daucus carota Seeds in Cognitive Function Improvement
abstract: This study evaluated the effects of Daucus carota seeds extract on cognitive functions, total serum cholesterol levels, and brain cholinesterase activity in mice. The ethanolic extract (DCE) was administered orally at doses of 100, 200, and 400 mg/kg for seven days to young and aged mice. Spatial memory tests and delayed matching tasks were used to assess cognitive performance. Diazepam-, scopolamine-, and age-related amnesia served as behavioral models. DCE at 200 and 400 mg/kg significantly improved memory scores in both age groups, with 23% and 35% increases, respectively. The extract reversed scopolamine-induced amnesia and diazepam-related cognitive impairments. DCE also reduced brain acetylcholinesterase activity and cholesterol levels, with 22% and 23% reductions in young and aged mice, respectively. These findings suggest that Daucus carota extract may be beneficial for managing cognitive dysfunctions due to its memory-enhancing, cholesterol-lowering, and anticholinesterase properties. Additional indexed biomedical mentions considered for relation extraction included: extract of Daucus carota seeds.

title: Mechanisms of hypertension associated with nitric oxide deficiency: venous function and oxidative stress
abstract: Nitric oxide (NO) deficiency is a key factor in the development of hypertension, particularly in the context of arterial dysfunction. Experimental models of hypertension induced by the administration of Nomega-nitro-L-arginine (LNNA) demonstrate that the loss of endothelial-derived NO leads to increased endothelin-1 (ET-1) release and heightened sympathetic nervous system activity. Rats were treated with LNNA (0.5 g/L in drinking water) for 2 weeks, resulting in a significant elevation of mean arterial pressure from 119 ± 2 mm Hg in control animals to 194 ± 5 mm Hg in LNNA-treated groups (P<0.05). Carotid arteries and vena cava were isolated for functional analysis, revealing that maximal contraction to norepinephrine was modestly reduced in arteries from LNNA-treated rats, while the response to ET-1 was significantly decreased (54% of control). In contrast, vena cava contraction to norepinephrine (37% of control) was reduced without a corresponding change in ET-1 response. Mean circulatory filling pressure, an indicator of venous smooth muscle tone, did not show significant changes in LNNA hypertension at 1 or 2 weeks post-treatment. The superoxide scavenger tempol (30, 100, and 300 micromol kg⁻¹, IV) did not alter arterial pressure in control rats but caused a dose-dependent reduction in LNNA-treated groups (-18 ± 8, -26 ± 15, and -54 ± 11 mm Hg). Ganglionic blockade with hexamethonium resulted in a more pronounced decrease in LNNA-induced hypertension (76 ± 9 mm Hg) compared to control rats (35 ± 10 mm Hg). Notably, LNNA-treated animals exhibited higher basal levels of superoxide in carotid arteries, vena cava, and sympathetic ganglia compared to controls. These findings suggest that while NO deficiency enhances oxidative stress and sympathetic activity in both arterial and venous vessels, the venous response does not significantly contribute to this form of hypertension. Additional indexed biomedical mentions considered for relation extraction included: NO synthase.

title: Efficacy of Eslicarbazepine Acetate in Treating Seizures Induced by Picrotoxin in Rats
abstract: Eslicarbazepine acetate (BIA 2-093) is a novel antiepileptic drug, structurally related to carbamazepine (CBZ) and oxcarbazepine (OXC), currently in Phase III trials for improved therapeutic profiles. This study evaluated its effects on seizures induced by picrotoxin in the hippocampus of freely moving rats. Oral administration of eslicarbazepine acetate at threshold doses of picrotoxin resulted in a 75% reduction in seizure occurrence, with significant decreases in seizure duration and frequency at 10 mg/kg. In contrast, lower doses (3 and 10 mg/kg) showed partial suppression of seizures. The compound demonstrated no adverse effects on sleep/wake patterns or EEG activity. These findings suggest a negative correlation between eslicarbazepine acetate and seizures, while picrotoxin exhibits a positive correlation with seizure induction. Comparative analysis revealed similar efficacy profiles between eslicarbazepine acetate and oxcarbazepine, though the former showed superior safety in this model.

title: Antioxidant effects of atorvastatin in dexamethasone-induced hypertension
abstract: Atorvastatin exhibits antioxidant properties in dexamethasone-induced hypertension, as demonstrated in a study on Sprague-Dawley rats. Dexamethasone-induced hypertension is marked by endothelial dysfunction, characterized by nitric oxide deficiency and elevated superoxide levels. Atorvastatin, known for its pleiotropic effects, enhances endothelial function by increasing nitric oxide availability and reducing superoxide production. In this experiment, rats were treated with atorvastatin (50 mg/kg/day) or placebo for 15 days, with dexamethasone administered after 4 days. Systolic blood pressure was monitored, and endothelial function was assessed via acetylcholine-induced vasorelaxation and phenylephrine-induced vasoconstriction. Vascular endothelial NO synthase mRNA expression was analyzed. Results showed that atorvastatin treatment reduced blood pressure and improved endothelial function compared to dexamethasone alone. Superoxide production was lower in the atorvastatin group, while nitric oxide levels were maintained. These findings highlight the role of atorvastatin in mitigating oxidative stress and endothelial dysfunction in dexamethasone-induced hypertension.

title: In Vitro Analysis of Receptor Modulation in Cyclophosphamide-Induced Cystitis
abstract: In vitro studies were conducted to evaluate the effects of muscarinic receptors and other receptor systems in cyclophosphamide-induced cystitis in rats. The expression and function of muscarinic receptors were altered in inflamed tissues, and their interactions with muscarinic , adrenergic and purinergic receptor antagonists were assessed. ATP and carbachol elicited similar responses in control and inflamed preparations, but isoprenaline-induced relaxations were reduced in the latter. Methoctramine, a muscarinic receptor antagonist, showed diminished efficacy in inflamed preparations, whereas atropine and 4-diphenylacetoxy-N-methylpiperidine (4-DAMP) partially reversed tonic contractions. Pirenzepine, another muscarinic receptor antagonist, exhibited reduced potency in inflamed tissues. Cyclophosphamide-induced changes also affected potassium responses, with alpha , beta-methylene adenosine-5'-triphosphate (alpha , beta-meATP) causing desensitization at low frequencies. Beta-adrenoceptor-mediated relaxations were diminished in inflamed strips, while prejunctional muscarinic receptor activity may be enhanced. These findings suggest that cystitis significantly alters efferent functional responses, particularly in receptor modulation.

title: Xanthine Oxidase and Nitric Oxide-Rhodamine in Glucocorticoid-Induced Hypertension
abstract: The role of xanthine oxidase in glucocorticoid-induced hypertension is explored through its interaction with nitric oxide-redox pathways. Glucocorticoid-induced hypertension (GC-HT) in rats is linked to nitric oxide-redox imbalance. This study investigates xanthine oxidase (XO), which contributes to reactive oxygen species production, in dexamethasone-induced hypertension (dex-HT). Thirty male Sprague-Dawley rats were divided into four groups: saline, dexamethasone, allopurinol plus saline, and allopurinol plus dexamethasone. Systolic blood pressure and body weights were measured every other day. Thymus weight, reflecting glucocorticoid activity, and serum urate, indicating XO inhibition, were monitored. Dexamethasone increased systolic blood pressure (110 ± 2 to 126 ± 3 mmHg; P < 0.001) and reduced thymus (P < 0.001) and body weights (P < 0.01). Allopurinol decreased serum urate from 76 ± 5 to 30 ± 3 micromol/L in saline and from 84 ± 13 to 28 ± 2 micromol/L in dex-treated groups (P < 0.001). Allopurinol did not prevent dex-HT. This finding, combined with prior results showing allopurinol's ineffectiveness against adrenocorticotrophic hormone-induced hypertension, suggests that XO activity is not a primary factor in GC-HT development in rats.

title: Neuroprotective Effects of Melatonin in BCNU-Induced Cortical Dysplasia
abstract: This study investigated the protective effects of melatonin against BCNU-induced cortical dysplasia in the rat model. Cortical dysplasia, characterized by impaired neural development, was examined in offspring following maternal exposure to BCNU. Experimental groups included intact-control, saline-control, melatonin-treated, BCNU-exposed, and BCNU-exposed plus melatonin. BCNU was administered on embryonic day 15, and melatonin was administered until delivery. Histological and biochemical analyses revealed that BCNU-exposed groups exhibited increased TUNEL-positive cells and reduced immunoreactivity to synaptophysin, glial fibrillary acidic protein, and transforming growth factor beta1. Melatonin treatment significantly reversed these changes, restoring normal protein expression. Malondialdehyde levels were elevated in BCNU-exposed groups, but melatonin treatment reduced malondialdehyde levels. Superoxide dismutase levels remained unchanged across all groups. Additionally, melatonin was associated with increased superoxide dismutase activity and a negative correlation with malondialdehyde. Superoxide levels were not significantly altered by BCNU or melatonin treatment.

title: Severe Rhabdomyolysis and Acute Renal Failure Due to Statin-CYP3A4 Inhibitor Interaction
abstract: A 68-year-old male with a history of hyperlipidemia, coronary artery disease, and atrial fibrillation presented with generalized fatigue, pain, and dark urine over 5 days. Laboratory findings revealed elevated creatine kinase (65,000 U/L), blood urea nitrogen (102 mg/dL), creatinine (5.1 mg/dL), aspartate aminotransferase (1800 U/L), and alanine aminotransferase (950 U/L). The patient was taking 40 mg simvastatin daily, 200 mg amiodarone daily, and 300 mg atazanavir daily. These medications were temporarily discontinued, and the patient received diuresis and dialysis. Nine days later, creatine kinase decreased to 1300 U/L, and creatinine normalized to 1.8 mg/dL. The case highlights the risk of rhabdomyolysis and acute renal failure from concomitant use of simvastatin and CYP3A4 inhibitors. Amiodarone and atazanavir are known CYP3A4 inhibitors, and simvastatin is metabolized by this enzyme. Pravastatin, fluvastatin, and rosuvastatin carry lower interaction risks compared to atorvastatin and simvastatin in patients on CYP3A4 inhibitors. Additional indexed biomedical mentions considered for relation extraction included: lovastatin.

title: Lamivudine-Resistant Hepatitis B Virus Strains in HIV Co-Infected Patients
abstract: This study examines the prevalence of lamivudine-resistant hepatitis B virus (HBV) strains in patients with and without HIV co-infection. Among 35 lamivudine-naive HBV infected individuals, 15 were chronic HBV mono-infected and 20 were HBV-HIV co-infected. The latter group was further divided into 13 occult HBV (HBsAg-negative) and 7 overt HBV (HBsAg-positive) patients. HBV viral load was measured using Amplicor HBV Monitor test v2.0 (Roche Diagnostics, Penzberg, Germany), and HBV reverse transcriptase (RT) primers were used for PCR amplification and direct sequencing of the YMDD motif in the C domain of the HBV RT enzyme. Lamivudine-resistant HBV strains were detected in 3 of 15 mono-infected patients and 10 of 20 co-infected patients. The study highlights the importance of monitoring HBV lamivudine resistance in HIV co-infected individuals, particularly those with HBsAg-negative status, to inform antiretroviral therapy strategies. Additional indexed biomedical mentions considered for relation extraction included: hepatitis B virus ( HBV ) infected; lamivudine-resistance.

title: Role of Adrenergic Receptors in Cocaine-Induced Anxiety
abstract: Norepinephrine signaling through beta-adrenergic receptors is essential for cocaine-induced anxiety. Cocaine-induced anxiety is a significant side effect of cocaine use, which is a commonly abused psychostimulant. While mechanisms behind cocaine's rewarding effects are well understood, the role of noradrenergic pathways in its aversive effects remains underexplored. In this study, dopamine beta-hydroxylase knockout (Dbh-/-) mice, which lack norepinephrine, were tested in the elevated plus maze (EPM) to assess the contribution of noradrenergic signaling to cocaine-induced anxiety. Cocaine dose-dependently increased anxiety-like behavior in control (Dbh+/-) mice, as evidenced by reduced open arm exploration. Dbh-/- mice showed normal baseline performance in the EPM but were resistant to cocaine's anxiogenic effects. Administration of disulfiram, a dopamine beta-hydroxylase inhibitor, reduced cocaine-induced anxiety in Dbh+/-. Using specific adrenergic antagonists, beta-adrenergic receptor antagonist propranolol blocked cocaine-induced anxiety in both Dbh+/- and wild-type mice, whereas alpha(1) antagonist prazosin and alpha(2) antagonist yohimbine had no effect. These findings highlight the critical role of beta-adrenergic receptors in mediating cocaine-induced anxiety. Additional indexed biomedical mentions considered for relation extraction included: alpha(2 ); alpha(1 ).

title: Comparative Effects of Lidocaine and Bupivacaine on Prostaglandin E2 and Pain in Postoperative Patients
abstract: This study investigated the differential impacts of lidocaine and bupivacaine on prostaglandin E2 release, cyclooxygenase gene expression, and pain following tissue injury in a clinical model. Patients undergoing third molar extraction received either 2% lidocaine or 0.5% bupivacaine before surgery, combined with rofecoxib 50 mg or placebo. Postoperative pain, measured via visual analog scale, showed distinct patterns: the bupivacaine/rofecoxib group experienced reduced pain initially, while the bupivacaine/placebo group reported increased pain at 24 hours. Prostaglandin E2 levels were significantly higher in the bupivacaine/placebo group during the first 4 hours, indicating a proinflammatory effect of bupivacaine. Thromboxane B2 levels remained unchanged, suggesting COX-2 inhibition rather than COX-1. Tissue injury was associated with elevated cyclooxygenase gene expression, particularly in the bupivacaine/placebo group. Thromboxane levels were not affected by any treatment, while postoperative pain correlated with prostaglandin E2 production. Inflammation was linked to increased cyclooxygenase activity, and tissue injury was found to stimulate prostaglandin E2 release. These findings highlight the complex interplay between local anesthetics, cyclooxygenase pathways, and postoperative pain management.

title: Clonidine in Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder: Safety and Tolerability Assessment
abstract: Clonidine was evaluated for its safety and tolerability in children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). A 16-week multicenter, double-blind trial enrolled 122 children, randomly assigned to clonidine (n=31), methylphenidate (n=29), clonidine plus methylphenidate (n=32), or placebo (n=30). Doses were titrated up to 0.6 mg/day for clonidine and 60 mg/day for methylphenidate. Adverse events and ECG changes were monitored. Clonidine was associated with a higher incidence of bradycardia compared to non-clonidine treatments, but no significant differences in other cardiovascular outcomes. Drowsiness was commonly reported with clonidine, typically resolving within 6-8 weeks. No interactions between clonidine and methylphenidate were observed regarding cardiovascular effects. Clonidine, used alone or in combination, was found to be safe and well-tolerated in pediatric ADHD patients.

title: Mechanisms of Azathioprine-Induced Anemia and Eryptosis
abstract: Azathioprine-induced anemia is associated with bone marrow suppression, which may result from accelerated eryptosis. Eryptosis is characterized by phosphatidylserine exposure on erythrocytes and cell shrinkage. Annexin V binding reflects this phosphatidylserine exposure, as observed in patients treated with azathioprine. Fluo3 fluorescence measures cytosolic Ca2+ activity, which increases in response to azathioprine exposure. In healthy volunteers, azathioprine (≥2 µg/mL) elevates Ca2+ activity and annexin V binding while reducing cell volume. The absence of extracellular Ca2+ diminishes these effects. These findings suggest that azathioprine triggers eryptosis, contributing to anemia through both bone marrow suppression and direct erythrocyte damage. Additional indexed biomedical mentions considered for relation extraction included: Ca2 +.

title: Role of Fractalkine Receptor Signaling in Neurotoxicity and Microglial Activation
abstract: Fractalkine receptor signaling does not mediate Methamphetamine-induced neurotoxicity or microglial activation. Methamphetamine (METH) induces dopamine (DA) neuronal damage through mechanisms involving microglial activation, but the specific pathways remain unclear. Recent studies identified the microglial-specific fractalkine receptor (CX3CR1) as critical for MPTP-induced neurodegeneration of DA neurons. Given that METH and MPTP cause selective DA neuronal damage in mouse models, we hypothesized CX3CR1 plays a role in METH-induced toxicity. Mice with CX3CR1 deleted and replaced by enhanced green fluorescent protein (eGFP) were treated with METH. METH depleted DA, activated microglia, and increased body temperature in CX3CR1 knockout mice similarly to wild-type controls. These effects were not gender-dependent and were confined to the striatum. Striatal microglia expressing eGFP showed morphological changes post-METH indicative of activation, distinct from unresponsive eGFP-microglia in non-damaged brain regions. These findings suggest CX3CR1 signaling does not modulate METH neurotoxicity or microglial activation. Additionally, striatal-resident microglia respond to METH via an activation cascade, reverting to a surveying state without apoptosis or migration.

title: Verapamil Modulation of Gastric Ulcer Pathogenesis in Atherosclerotic Rats
abstract: This study investigates the protective effects of verapamil on gastric hemorrhagic ulcers in atherosclerotic rats. Atherosclerosis was induced in male Wistar rats through daily intragastric administration of corn oil containing vitamin D2 and cholesterol. Control rats received corn oil alone. Gastric surgery was followed by 3-hour irrigation with simulated gastric juice or normal saline. Measurements included gastric acid back-diffusion, lipid peroxide generation, histamine concentration, microvascular permeability, luminal hemoglobin content, and ulcer area. Atherosclerotic rats exhibited elevated serum calcium, total cholesterol, and low-density lipoprotein levels. Severe gastric ulcers were associated with increased acid back-diffusion, histamine release, lipid peroxide production, and luminal hemoglobin. A positive correlation between histamine and ulcer severity was observed. Daily verapamil treatment significantly reduced these ulcerogenic factors, suggesting its role in ameliorating atherosclerosis-induced gastric damage. The study highlights the potential of verapamil to counteract gastric ulcer formation through modulation of key pathophysiological mechanisms.

title: High Fat Diet-Induced Obesity Enhances Sensitivity to Doxorubicin-Induced Cardiotoxicity
abstract: Rats fed a 40% high fat diet (HFD) to induce obesity exhibit heightened susceptibility to doxorubicin-induced cardiotoxicity. This study investigated the effects of HFD on doxorubicin toxicity, revealing that obese rats showed increased cardiac dysfunction and lipid peroxidation following a single dose of doxorubicin. Notably, no significant renal or hepatic toxicity was observed, despite the observed cardiotoxicity. Mechanistic analyses demonstrated that HFD-induced obesity was associated with elevated oxidative stress, upregulated uncoupling proteins 2 and 3, and reduced cardiac fatty-acid oxidation. Additionally, decreased plasma adiponectin levels, downregulated peroxisome proliferators activated receptor-alpha, and diminished mitochondrial AMP-alpha2 protein kinase activity contributed to the observed cardiotoxic effects. Cardiac ATP levels were significantly reduced, with a corresponding drop in the ATP/ADP ratio, while decreased erythropoietin and increased SOCS3 further impaired the JAK/STAT3 pathway. These findings underscore the critical role of metabolic alterations in mediating doxorubicin-induced cardiotoxicity in obese individuals. Additional indexed biomedical mentions considered for relation extraction included: triglycerides; doxorubicinol.

title: Simvastatin-Ezetimibe-Induced Hepatotoxicity and Liver Failure
abstract: Simvastatin-ezetimibe-induced hepatotoxicity and liver failure are rare but severe adverse effects of combination therapy. A 68-year-old African American man developed fulminant hepatic failure requiring liver transplantation 8 weeks after switching from atorvastatin 80 mg/day to simvastatin-ezetimibe 10 mg/40 mg/day. His lipid profile had been stable with atorvastatin for 19 months without prior hepatotoxicity. A routine lab test 8 weeks after the switch showed elevated serum aminotransferase levels. Simvastatin-ezetimibe and paroxetine (used for depression) were discontinued, and other causes of hepatotoxicity were ruled out. A repeat test revealed further increases in aminotransferase levels, and a liver biopsy showed moderate-to-severe drug toxicity. He underwent liver transplantation with a complication-free recovery. His aminotransferase levels normalized by postoperative day 22, and a 2-year follow-up showed no further issues. Ezetimibe is extensively metabolized by uridine diphosphate glucuronosyltransferases (UGT) in the gut and liver, and may have inhibited UGT activity in simvastatin hydroxy acid, leading to increased simvastatin levels and hepatotoxicity. This is the first reported case of simvastatin-ezetimibe-induced liver failure requiring transplantation. We propose that the mechanism involves ezetimibe's inhibition of UGT enzymes, increasing simvastatin exposure. Clinicians should be cautious about hepatotoxicity in elderly patients and monitor serum aminotransferase levels closely when initiating or adjusting simvastatin-ezetimibe therapy. Additional indexed biomedical mentions considered for relation extraction included: escitalopram; 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl coenzyme A reductase; uridine diphosphate glucoronosyltransferases; statin; hepatotoxic.

title: Bisphosphonate-Induced Proteinuria and Renal Complications in Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis
abstract: A 62-year-old man with focal segmental glomerulosclerosis and nephrotic syndrome was treated with steroid therapy, which initially reduced his urinary protein from 16.2 to 3.1 g. Following oral administration of bisphosphonate (alendronate), his urinary protein rose sharply to 13.5 g within two weeks, leading to acute renal failure. After stopping the bisphosphonate, the patient underwent five cycles of hemodialysis and three cycles of LDL apheresis. Urinary volume and serum creatinine levels normalized, with proteinuria resolving in 45 days. Creatinine levels were monitored throughout, showing no significant correlation with bisphosphonate use. Alendronate was associated with increased proteinuria but not directly with creatinine levels. Steroid use did not show a direct correlation with acute renal failure in this case.

title: Sulphonylurea Treatment and Coronary Artery Disease Risk in Type 2 Diabetes Patients
abstract: This study evaluates the association between initial sulphonylurea treatment and the risk of coronary artery disease (CAD) in patients with type 2 diabetes. A matched case-control analysis was conducted, comparing 76 cases of CAD with 152 controls without CAD. The 20-year CAD risk at diabetes diagnosis, calculated using the UKPDS risk engine, was used to ensure comparable follow-up periods. Results show that treatment with glibenclamide was linked to a 2.4-fold increased hazard of CAD (95% CI 1.3-4.3, P=0.004), while glipizide was associated with a 2-fold increase (95% CI 0.9-4.6, P=0.099). Metformin treatment showed no significant change in CAD risk. In contrast, glimepiride and gliclazide were associated with a 0.3-fold and 0.4-fold decrease in CAD hazard, respectively. These findings suggest that glibenclamide and glipizide may pose a higher risk for CAD compared to glimepiride and gliclazide. The study highlights the importance of selecting sulphonylureas with lower cardiovascular risk, particularly in populations where these agents are commonly prescribed.

title: Losartan Therapy in Adriamycin-Induced Nephropathy
abstract: This study examined the effects of losartan on the progression of adriamycin-induced nephropathy in spontaneously hypertensive rats. The treatment significantly reduced the development of glomerulosclerosis and tubular atrophy, which were associated with decreased proteinuria and interstitial fibrosis. Losartan also ameliorated chronic renal failure and prevented the progression to uraemia by improving urea clearance. The drug's impact on angiotensin II type-1 receptor activity was linked to reduced focal segmental glomerulosclerosis and improved renal function. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of losartan in slowing disease progression. Urea levels were closely monitored, and the relationship between urea and interstitial fibrosis remained uncorrelated. Chronic renal failure showed no direct association with urea, while nephropathy was inversely related to losartan treatment. The study also observed a positive correlation between adriamycin exposure and focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, with losartan treatment reducing this correlation. No significant associations were found between urea and glomerulosclerosis, or between urea and angiotensin II type-1 receptor activity. Losartan's effect on proteinuria was independent of its interaction with angiotensin II type-1 receptor, and no direct correlation was observed between losartan and hypertensive conditions. The relationship between adriamycin and nephropathy was confirmed, as well as the inverse correlation between losartan and interstitial fibrosis. Uraemia and chronic renal failure were not directly correlated with urea, and no association was found between urea and atrophy. The study also noted that losartan's effect on proteinuria was independent of its interaction with angiotensin II type-1 receptor, and no direct correlation was observed between losartan and hypertensive conditions.

title: Synergistic Effects of Green Tea and Vitamin E in Isoproterenol-Induced Myocardial Infarction in Rats
abstract: This study examined the combined impact of green tea and vitamin E on cardiac and systemic parameters in isoproterenol (ISO)-induced myocardial infarction in rats. Adult male albino rats were administered ISO (200 mg/kg, s.c.) for two days, leading to significant (P<0.05) increases in heart weight, serum enzymes, lipid peroxidation, and Ca+2 ATPase levels, alongside notable decreases in body weight, endogenous antioxidants, Na+/K+ ATPase, and Mg+2 ATPase. Concurrent treatment with green tea (100 mg/kg/day, p.o.) and vitamin E (100 mg/kg/day, p.o.) for 30 days, followed by ISO challenge on days 29 and 30, resulted in significant (P<0.05) reductions in heart weight, serum enzymes, lipid peroxidation, and Ca+2 ATPase, along with increased body weight, antioxidants, Na+/K+ ATPase, and Mg+2 ATPase compared to ISO-only or single-agent groups. These results highlight the protective synergy of green tea and vitamin E against ISO-induced myocardial injury, with vitamin E showing a negative correlation with lipid levels and a positive correlation with Na+/K+ ATPase. Antioxidants exhibited no direct relation to Ca+2 ATPase, while green tea demonstrated a positive correlation with Mg+2 ATPase and a negative correlation with lipid peroxidation. The association between isoproterenol and myocardial infarction was confirmed, with no significant relation between antioxidants and Na+/K+ ATPase observed. Additional indexed biomedical mentions considered for relation extraction included: Na+/ K+ ATPase.

title: Antioxidant and Cardioprotective Effects of Salvianolic Acid A in Isoproterenol-Induced Myocardial Injury
abstract: This study investigates the cardioprotective effects of salvianolic acid A in isoproterenol-induced myocardial injury in rats. The experiment aimed to assess the protective potential of salvianolic acid A against isoproterenol-induced myocardial injury. Hemodynamic parameters and electrocardiogram recordings were continuously monitored. Serum and cardiac tissue levels of cardiac marker enzymes and antioxidant parameters were measured. Mitochondrial respiratory function assays and histopathological analysis of heart tissues were conducted. Rats treated with isoproterenol exhibited significant increases in lactate dehydrogenase, aspartate transaminase, creatine kinase, and malondialdehyde levels, along with decreased superoxide dismutase, catalase, and glutathione peroxidase activities in serum and heart tissues. These animals also showed reduced left ventricular systolic pressure, decreased maximum and minimum rate of pressure development, and elevated left ventricular end-diastolic pressure and ST-segment elevation. Mitochondrial respiratory dysfunction was observed, characterized by reduced respiratory control ratio and ADP/O. Administration of salvianolic acid A for 8 days significantly improved isoproterenol-induced cardiac dysfunction and myocardial injury, restoring mitochondrial respiratory function. Histopathological examination confirmed the protective effects of salvianolic acid A against isoproterenol-induced myocardial damage. The results indicate that salvianolic acid A, with its antioxidant properties, significantly protects against isoproterenol-induced myocardial injury. Additional indexed biomedical mentions considered for relation extraction included: myocardial infarction.

title: Neurological Impacts of Ecstasy and Cannabis Use on Cognitive Functions
abstract: Ecstasy users exhibit hyperactivity and Learning and memory deficits, which are associated with neurotoxic effects. Cannabis users also show Learning and memory deficits, though the relationship between cannabis and neurotoxicity is not established. A study compared ecstasy users with cannabis users, revealing that ecstasy users performed worse in learning and memory tasks. Functional imaging showed ecstasy-specific hyperactivity in frontal and temporal regions, while hypoactivity was observed in the dorsal anterior cingulated cortex. Both groups showed reduced activation in medial frontal and parahippocampal regions, indicating potential neurotoxic impacts of ecstasy, with cannabis use possibly contributing to some deficits.

title: Lithium-Induced Polyuria and mPGES-1 Deficiency in Mice: A Comparative Study
abstract: Mice deficient in mPGES-1 show resistance to lithium-induced polyuria. Cyclooxygenase-2 activity is essential for the development of lithium-induced polyuria. However, the role of a specific terminal prostaglandin (PG) isomerase remains unexplored. This study evaluates lithium-induced polyuria in mice lacking microsomal prostaglandin E synthase-1 (mPGES-1). Two-week administration of LiCl (4 mmol.kg(-1).day(-1) ip) in mPGES-1 +/+ mice resulted in marked polyuria with hyposmotic urine. This was accompanied by increased renal mPGES-1 protein and elevated urine PGE(2) excretion. In contrast, mPGES-1 -/- mice exhibited resistance to lithium-induced polyuria and urine concentrating defects, along with near-complete inhibition of PGE(2) and cAMP output. Immunoblotting, immunohistochemistry, and qRT-PCR revealed significant decreases in aquaporin-2 (AQP2) protein expression in both renal cortex and medulla of lithium-treated +/+ mice. This decrease was significantly reduced in -/- mice. qRT-PCR detected similar AQP2 mRNA changes in the medulla but not the cortex. Similarly, total medullary Na-K-2Cl cotransporter (NKCC2) protein abundance was significantly reduced in +/+ mice, but this was attenuated in -/- mice. These findings suggest that mPGES-1-derived PGE(2) mediates lithium-induced polyuria through inhibition of AQP2 and NKCC2 expression. Additional indexed biomedical mentions considered for relation extraction included: PGE(2 ).

title: Mechanisms of Pilocarpine in Modulating Arrhythmias and Calcium Handling
abstract: This study investigates the antiarrhythmic properties and ionic mechanisms of pilocarpine in animal models. Using aconitine-induced rat and ouabain-induced guinea pig arrhythmia models, we evaluated the effects of pilocarpine on arrhythmic conditions. Confocal microscopy revealed that pilocarpine significantly delayed the onset of arrhythmias, reduced the duration of ventricular tachycardia and fibrillation, and improved survival rates in arrhythmic animals. The study also demonstrated that pilocarpine decreased [Ca(2+)](i) overload caused by aconitine or ouabain in isolated myocytes. Additionally, the M(3)-muscarinic acetylcholine receptor (mAChR) antagonist 4-DAMP partially reversed the beneficial effects of pilocarpine, suggesting that the antiarrhythmic actions are mediated through mAChR activation. The results indicate that pilocarpine may enhance Ca(2+) handling and reduce arrhythmia severity in these models. Furthermore, the relationship between pilocarpine and free-calcium was characterized as a negative correlation, while the interaction between aconitine-induced and arrhythmia was associated with a positive correlation. The M(3)-muscarinic acetylcholine receptor was linked to both pilocarpine and 4-DAMP through an association, and the effects of ouabain-induced on arrhythmia were linked via a positive correlation.

title: Nimodipine Mitigates Memory Impairment in Nitroglycerin-Induced Hypotension
abstract: Nimodipine alleviates memory impairment associated with nitroglycerin-induced hypotension in adult mice. BACKGROUND: Hypotension and reduced cerebral blood flow contribute to cognitive dysfunction. We hypothesized that nimodipine administered during nitroglycerin-induced hypotension would preserve long-term memory. METHODS: The passive avoidance paradigm assessed memory retention. Latencies for entering a shock chamber were measured before and after a 48-hour interval. Ninety-six mice were divided into groups: saline, nitroglycerin immediately post-learning, nitroglycerin 3 hours post-learning, nitroglycerin plus nimodipine, vehicle, and nimodipine alone. Hypotension severity and brain oxygenation were analyzed in another group. RESULTS: All groups showed similar training latencies.
